A parabola is its own mirror image in one vertical line, and the abscissa of that line is settled by the first two coefficients alone.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$p(x)=2x^{2}-8$$

$$x=-\frac{0}{2\cdot 2}=0$$

The mirror line is $x=0$ while the claim names $x=1$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

A parabola reaches its extreme value at the turning point and nowhere else, so locate the axis first and then read the height there.

$$p(x)=2x^{2}-8$$

$$x=-\frac{0}{2\cdot 2}=0$$

$$p(0)=2\cdot 0^{2}-8=-8$$

The leading coefficient $2$ is positive, so the arms rise on both sides and $-8$ is the smallest value the function ever takes; there is no largest one.

That extreme value is $-8$, exactly as claimed, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
There is one graph to study, and it is a parabola.

$$p(x)=2x^{2}-8$$

The axis formula fixes the turning point, while the sum $S$ and the product $P$ of the roots come out of the coefficients with no equation to solve.

$$\text{vertex}=\left(0,-8\right)\qquad S=0\qquad P=-4$$

Two real roots follow from the positive discriminant, and the axis of symmetry sits exactly halfway between them.

$$\Delta=64\qquad x_{1}=-2\qquad x_{2}=2$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-8$.

tasks.title: A Parabola That Turns Downwards
tasks.context: Consider the quadratic function $q(x)=-3x^{2}+12x-4$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graph of $q$ opens downwards.
The axis of symmetry of $q$ is the line $x=2$.
The largest value taken by $q$ is $8$.
The graph of $q$ meets the $y$-axis at $y=4$.
The equation $q(x)=0$ has two distinct real solutions.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Far away from the turning point the square term dwarfs the rest, so the sign of the leading coefficient decides on its own which way the arms point.

$$q(x)=-3x^{2}+12x-4$$

$$a=-3$$

A negative leading coefficient sends both arms downwards, and the turning point is the highest point of the graph.

The graph opens downwards, which is what the claim says, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A parabola is its own mirror image in one vertical line, and the abscissa of that line is settled by the first two coefficients alone.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$q(x)=-3x^{2}+12x-4$$

$$x=-\frac{12}{2\cdot \left(-3\right)}=2$$

The mirror line is $x=2$, exactly the line named in the claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

A parabola reaches its extreme value at the turning point and nowhere else, so locate the axis first and then read the height there.

$$q(x)=-3x^{2}+12x-4$$

$$x=-\frac{12}{2\cdot \left(-3\right)}=2$$

$$q(2)=-3\cdot 2^{2}+12\cdot 2-4=8$$

The leading coefficient $-3$ is negative, so the arms fall on both sides and $8$ is the largest value the function ever takes; there is no smallest one.

That extreme value is $8$, exactly as claimed, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The graph meets the $y$-axis where the input is zero, so the intercept is simply the constant term of the rule.

$$q(x)=-3x^{2}+12x-4$$

$$q(0)=-3\cdot 0^{2}+12\cdot 0-4=-4$$

The graph cuts the $y$-axis at $y=-4$ while the claim names $y=4$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The number of real solutions of a quadratic equation is decided by the discriminant, the expression under the square root of the solution formula.

$$\Delta=b^{2}-4ac$$

$$q(x)=-3x^{2}+12x-4$$

$$\Delta=12^{2}-4\left(-3\right)\left(-4\right)=96$$

A discriminant that is positive means the equation has two distinct real solutions.

There are two distinct real solutions, which is what the claim says, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Everything below refers to the same parabola.

$$q(x)=-3x^{2}+12x-4$$

Before testing anything, it pays to write down the vertex together with the sum and the product of the roots, all three being coefficient arithmetic.

$$\text{vertex}=\left(2,8\right)\qquad S=4\qquad P=\frac{4}{3}$$

A positive discriminant puts two crossings on the $x$-axis.

$$\Delta=96$$

The arms open downwards, so the turning point is the highest point of the graph and the largest value is $8$.

tasks.title: Vertex Form Read at a Glance
tasks.context: A parabola is already written in completed-square form: $p(x)=\left(x+3\right)^{2}-7$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The vertex of the graph of $p$ is the point $\left(-3,-7\right)$.
The axis of symmetry of $p$ is the line $x=3$.
The graph of $p$ opens upwards.
The smallest value taken by $p$ is $-7$.
Expanding gives $p(x)=x^{2}+6x+2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The turning point lies on the axis of symmetry, so its abscissa comes from the coefficients and its height is the value of the function there.

$$p(x)=x^{2}+6x+2$$

$$x=-\frac{6}{2\cdot 1}=-3$$

Evaluating on the axis gives the height.

$$p\left(-3\right)=\left(-3\right)^{2}+6\cdot \left(-3\right)+2=-7$$

The turning point is $\left(-3,-7\right)$, the point the claim names, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

A parabola is its own mirror image in one vertical line, and the abscissa of that line is settled by the first two coefficients alone.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}+6x+2$$

$$x=-\frac{6}{2\cdot 1}=-3$$

The mirror line is $x=-3$ while the claim names $x=3$, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Far away from the turning point the square term dwarfs the rest, so the sign of the leading coefficient decides on its own which way the arms point.

$$p(x)=x^{2}+6x+2$$

$$a=1$$

A positive leading coefficient sends both arms upwards, and the turning point is the lowest point of the graph.

The graph opens upwards, which is what the claim says, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

A parabola reaches its extreme value at the turning point and nowhere else, so locate the axis first and then read the height there.

$$p(x)=x^{2}+6x+2$$

$$x=-\frac{6}{2\cdot 1}=-3$$

$$p\left(-3\right)=\left(-3\right)^{2}+6\cdot \left(-3\right)+2=-7$$

The leading coefficient $1$ is positive, so the arms rise on both sides and $-7$ is the smallest value the function ever takes; there is no largest one.

That extreme value is $-7$, exactly as claimed, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Expanding means multiplying every bracket out and collecting equal powers of $x$; nothing else about the function changes.

$$p(x)=\left(x+3\right)^{2}-7$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}+6x+2$$

Every coefficient of the expansion can now be compared with the one the claim displays.

The two rules agree in all three coefficients, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The stem fixes a single parabola.

$$p(x)=\left(x+3\right)^{2}-7$$

Multiplying out puts the same rule in standard form, where every coefficient can be read off directly.

$$p(x)=x^{2}+6x+2$$

The completed square hands over the turning point, and Vieta's relations hand over the sum and the product of the roots.

$$\text{vertex}=\left(-3,-7\right)\qquad S=-6\qquad P=2$$

A positive discriminant puts two crossings on the $x$-axis.

$$\Delta=28$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-7$.

tasks.title: Zeros Straight From a Product of Factors
tasks.context: A quadratic function is handed over already factored: $q(x)=\left(x-1\right)\left(x+6\right)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The roots of $q$ are $1$ and $-6$.
The two roots of $q$ add up to $-5$.
The graph of $q$ opens downwards.
The graph of $q$ meets the $y$-axis at $y=-6$.
Expanding gives $q(x)=x^{2}+5x-6$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The roots are the inputs where the graph touches the $x$-axis, so set the rule equal to zero; the discriminant says first how many such inputs exist.

$$q(x)=x^{2}+5x-6$$

$$\Delta=5^{2}-4\left(1\right)\left(-6\right)=49$$

A positive discriminant gives two separate roots, delivered by the quadratic formula.

$$x_{1}=-6\qquad x_{2}=1$$

The zeros are $-6$ and $1$, the pair named in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Vieta's relations read the sum of the two roots straight off the coefficients, with no equation to solve: it is minus the middle coefficient divided by the leading one.

$$S=-\frac{b}{a}$$

$$q(x)=x^{2}+5x-6$$

$$S=-\frac{5}{1}=-5$$

The roots themselves are $-6$ and $1$, and they do add up to $-5$.

The sum is $-5$, the number the claim reports, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Far away from the turning point the square term dwarfs the rest, so the sign of the leading coefficient decides on its own which way the arms point.

$$q(x)=x^{2}+5x-6$$

$$a=1$$

A positive leading coefficient sends both arms upwards, and the turning point is the lowest point of the graph.

The graph opens upwards, not downwards, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The graph meets the $y$-axis where the input is zero, so the intercept is simply the constant term of the rule.

$$q(x)=x^{2}+5x-6$$

$$q(0)=0^{2}+5\cdot 0-6=-6$$

The graph cuts the $y$-axis at $y=-6$, the height the claim names, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Expanding means multiplying every bracket out and collecting equal powers of $x$; nothing else about the function changes.

$$q(x)=\left(x-1\right)\left(x+6\right)$$

$$q(x)=x^{2}+5x-6$$

Every coefficient of the expansion can now be compared with the one the claim displays.

The two rules agree in all three coefficients, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Only one parabola is in play here.

$$q(x)=\left(x-1\right)\left(x+6\right)$$

Multiplying out puts the same rule in standard form, where every coefficient can be read off directly.

$$q(x)=x^{2}+5x-6$$

Completing the square locates the turning point, and Vieta's relations give the sum $S$ and the product $P$ of the roots without solving anything.

$$\text{vertex}=\left(-\frac{5}{2},-\frac{49}{4}\right)\qquad S=-5\qquad P=-6$$

The discriminant comes out positive, so the graph cuts the $x$-axis twice, once on either side of the axis of symmetry.

$$\Delta=49\qquad x_{1}=-6\qquad x_{2}=1$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-\frac{49}{4}$.

tasks.title: A Water Tank Draining at a Steady Rate
tasks.context: A tank drains at a steady rate: after $x$ minutes it still holds $V(x)=200-8x$ litres. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Each extra minute changes the volume by $-8$ litres.
At $x=10$ the volume equals $120$ litres.
The volume equals $0$ litres at $x=25$.
Doubling $x$ always doubles the volume.
The volume changes by the same amount for every extra minute.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The model is linear, so one extra minute always changes the volume by the same amount, and that amount is the slope.

$$V(x)=-8x+200$$

$$V(x+1)-V(x)=\left(-8\left(x+1\right)+200\right)-\left(-8x+200\right)=-8$$

Each extra minute moves the volume by $-8$, as claimed, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The model turns any input into the volume, so a claim about one particular input is settled by a single substitution.

$$V(x)=-8x+200$$

$$V(10)=-8\cdot 10+200=120$$

The model returns $120$ there, the figure named in the claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The claim pins the volume to one figure, so read the model as an equation and see which input produces that figure.

$$-8x+200=0$$

$$-8x=-200$$

$$x=25$$

Substituting the claimed input back into the model checks the pair.

$$V(25)=-8\cdot 25+200=0$$

The volume at that input really is $0$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Doubling the input doubles the output only for a model whose graph runs through the origin; a constant term is charged once and is not doubled with the rest.

$$V(x)=-8x+200$$

$$V(1)=-8\cdot 1+200=192$$

$$V(2)=-8\cdot 2+200=184$$

Twice the value at $x=1$ would be $384$, whereas the model gives $184$ at $x=2$.

The constant term $200$ survives the doubling and breaks the proportion between $x$ and the volume, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Equal steps of the input produce equal changes of the volume only when the model is a line; a square term makes the steps grow.

$$V(x)=-8x+200$$

$$V(x+1)-V(x)=-8$$

The difference does not contain $x$ any more, so every extra minute counts the same.

The change per step is the constant slope, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The stem fixes a single line.

$$V(x)=200-8x$$

Ordering the two terms brings the rule into the shape $mx+q$.

$$V(x)=-8x+200$$

Two numbers describe it completely: the slope, which is the change of height per unit step, and the height above the origin.

$$m=-8\qquad V(0)=200$$

Setting the height to zero locates the single crossing of the $x$-axis, and the sign of the slope fixes the direction once and for all.

$$-8x+200=0\Rightarrow x=25$$

tasks.title: Where a Rising Line Crosses the Axes
tasks.context: Let $u(x)=4x+10$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graph of $u$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x=-\frac{5}{2}$.
The graph of $u$ meets the $y$-axis at $y=10$.
The slope of the graph of $u$ is $10$.
$u$ is increasing.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The graph crosses the $x$-axis where the height is zero, so set the rule equal to zero and solve the linear equation.

$$4x+10=0$$

$$4x=-10$$

$$x=\frac{-10}{4}=-\frac{5}{2}$$

The crossing is at $x=-\frac{5}{2}$, exactly where the claim puts it, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The graph meets the $y$-axis where the input is zero, so the intercept is simply the constant term of the rule.

$$u(x)=4x+10$$

$$u(0)=4\cdot 0+10=10$$

The graph cuts the $y$-axis at $y=10$, the height the claim names, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

A line written as $mx+q$ shows both of its numbers openly: $m$ is the slope and $q$ is the height above the origin.

$$u(x)=4x+10$$

$$m=4\qquad q=10$$

Stepping one unit to the right changes the height by $4$, the same everywhere along the line.

The slope is $4$ while the claim reports $10$; the other number, $10$, is the intercept, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

A line has the same steepness everywhere, so its direction is decided once and for all by the sign of the slope.

$$u(x)=4x+10$$

$$m=4$$

Because the slope is positive, every step to the right raises the height.

The function is increasing, as claimed, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Evaluating a function means putting the number in place of every $x$ and working the arithmetic out once.

$$u(x)=4x+10$$

$$u(3)=4\cdot 3+10=22$$

The graph therefore passes through the point $\left(3,22\right)$.

The value is $22$, precisely the number in the claim, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The stem fixes a single line.

$$u(x)=4x+10$$

Two numbers describe it completely: the slope, which is the change of height per unit step, and the height above the origin.

$$m=4\qquad u(0)=10$$

Setting the height to zero locates the single crossing of the $x$-axis, and the sign of the slope fixes the direction once and for all.

$$4x+10=0\Rightarrow x=-\frac{5}{2}$$

tasks.title: Locating the Peak of a Downward Parabola
tasks.context: The function $h$ is given by $h(x)=-x^{2}+6x-5$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graph of $h$ opens downwards.
The axis of symmetry of $h$ is the line $x=3$.
The largest value taken by $h$ is $4$.
The graph of $h$ meets the $y$-axis at $y=5$.
The roots of $h$ are $1$ and $5$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Far away from the turning point the square term dwarfs the rest, so the sign of the leading coefficient decides on its own which way the arms point.

$$h(x)=-x^{2}+6x-5$$

$$a=-1$$

A negative leading coefficient sends both arms downwards, and the turning point is the highest point of the graph.

The graph opens downwards, which is what the claim says, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A parabola is its own mirror image in one vertical line, and the abscissa of that line is settled by the first two coefficients alone.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$h(x)=-x^{2}+6x-5$$

$$x=-\frac{6}{2\cdot \left(-1\right)}=3$$

The mirror line is $x=3$, exactly the line named in the claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

A parabola reaches its extreme value at the turning point and nowhere else, so locate the axis first and then read the height there.

$$h(x)=-x^{2}+6x-5$$

$$x=-\frac{6}{2\cdot \left(-1\right)}=3$$

$$h(3)=-3^{2}+6\cdot 3-5=4$$

The leading coefficient $-1$ is negative, so the arms fall on both sides and $4$ is the largest value the function ever takes; there is no smallest one.

That extreme value is $4$, exactly as claimed, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The graph meets the $y$-axis where the input is zero, so the intercept is simply the constant term of the rule.

$$h(x)=-x^{2}+6x-5$$

$$h(0)=-0^{2}+6\cdot 0-5=-5$$

The graph cuts the $y$-axis at $y=-5$ while the claim names $y=5$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The roots are the inputs where the graph touches the $x$-axis, so set the rule equal to zero; the discriminant says first how many such inputs exist.

$$h(x)=-x^{2}+6x-5$$

$$\Delta=6^{2}-4\left(-1\right)\left(-5\right)=16$$

A positive discriminant gives two separate roots, delivered by the quadratic formula.

$$x_{1}=1\qquad x_{2}=5$$

The zeros are $1$ and $5$, the pair named in the claim, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Everything below refers to the same parabola.

$$h(x)=-x^{2}+6x-5$$

Before testing anything, it pays to write down the vertex together with the sum and the product of the roots, all three being coefficient arithmetic.

$$\text{vertex}=\left(3,4\right)\qquad S=6\qquad P=5$$

A positive discriminant puts two crossings on the $x$-axis, placed symmetrically around the axis of the parabola.

$$\Delta=16\qquad x_{1}=1\qquad x_{2}=5$$

The arms open downwards, so the turning point is the highest point of the graph and the largest value is $4$.

tasks.title: A Gentle Slope in Fraction Form
tasks.context: The line $v$ is given by $v(x)=\frac{1}{3}x-2$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The slope of the graph of $v$ is $\frac{1}{3}$.
The graph of $v$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x=6$.
The graph of $v$ meets the $y$-axis at $y=-2$.
Increasing $x$ by $3$ always changes $v$ by $1$.
$v$ is decreasing.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A line written as $mx+q$ shows both of its numbers openly: $m$ is the slope and $q$ is the height above the origin.

$$v(x)=\frac{1}{3}x-2$$

$$m=\frac{1}{3}\qquad q=-2$$

Stepping one unit to the right changes the height by $\frac{1}{3}$, the same everywhere along the line.

The slope is $\frac{1}{3}$, the number the claim reports, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The graph crosses the $x$-axis where the height is zero, so set the rule equal to zero and solve the linear equation.

$$\frac{1}{3}x-2=0$$

$$\frac{1}{3}x=2$$

$$x=2\cdot 3=6$$

The crossing is at $x=6$, exactly where the claim puts it, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The graph meets the $y$-axis where the input is zero, so the intercept is simply the constant term of the rule.

$$v(x)=\frac{1}{3}x-2$$

$$v(0)=\frac{1}{3}\cdot 0-2=-2$$

The graph cuts the $y$-axis at $y=-2$, the height the claim names, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

On a line the change of height depends only on the length of the step, never on where the step starts: it is the slope times that length.

$$v(x)=\frac{1}{3}x-2$$

$$v\left(x+3\right)-v(x)=\frac{1}{3}\cdot 3=1$$

A step of $3$ changes the height by $1$, as claimed, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

A line has the same steepness everywhere, so its direction is decided once and for all by the sign of the slope.

$$v(x)=\frac{1}{3}x-2$$

$$m=\frac{1}{3}$$

Because the slope is positive, every step to the right raises the height.

The function is increasing, not decreasing, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The stem fixes a single line.

$$v(x)=\frac{1}{3}x-2$$

Two numbers describe it completely: the slope, which is the change of height per unit step, and the height above the origin.

$$m=\frac{1}{3}\qquad v(0)=-2$$

Setting the height to zero locates the single crossing of the $x$-axis, and the sign of the slope fixes the direction once and for all.

$$\frac{1}{3}x-2=0\Rightarrow x=6$$

tasks.title: Constant Second Differences in a Table
tasks.context: A function was sampled at five consecutive whole numbers and the results were collected in the table below. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The first differences of the $y$-values are constant.
The second differences of the $y$-values are constant and equal to $2$.
The table is consistent with a quadratic model.
The table is produced by the rule $y=x^{2}+1$.
Continuing the pattern, the value at $x=5$ is $26$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

With equally spaced inputs the differences of neighbouring outputs do all the work: constant first differences are the fingerprint of a line.

$$y:\ 1,\ 2,\ 5,\ 10,\ 17$$

$$\text{first differences}:\ 1,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7$$

The steps come in different sizes, which is exactly what non-constant first differences mean, so the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Differencing twice is the standard test for a parabola: the second differences of a quadratic rule are constant, and they are zero for a line.

$$\text{first differences}:\ 1,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7$$

$$\text{second differences}:\ 2,\ 2,\ 2$$

They are all equal to $2$, the value the claim names, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

A table is consistent with a line when its first differences are constant, and with a parabola when the second differences are constant while the first ones are not.

$$\text{first differences}:\ 1,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7$$

$$\text{second differences}:\ 2,\ 2,\ 2$$

$$y=x^{2}+1$$

The pattern is exactly the one a quadratic rule produces, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Testing a proposed rule against a table is a matter of substitution: the rule has to reproduce every row, and for a rule of degree at most two three rows already pin it down.

$$y=x^{2}+1$$

Running the claimed rule over the first rows gives

$$0\mapsto 1,\quad 1\mapsto 2,\quad 2\mapsto 5$$

Every row comes out right, which identifies the claimed rule as the one behind the table, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Continuing a table means continuing its rule, so identify the rule from the differences first and only then step one row further.

$$y=x^{2}+1$$

$$y(5)=5^{2}+1=26$$

The next row would read $26$, exactly the value claimed, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The table is the whole stem, so read it as a list of pairs.

$$\left(0,1\right),\ \left(1,2\right),\ \left(2,5\right),\ \left(3,10\right),\ \left(4,17\right)$$

The inputs are equally spaced, which makes the differences of neighbouring outputs the fastest diagnostic tool available.

$$\text{first}:\ 1,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7\qquad \text{second}:\ 2,\ 2,\ 2$$

The first differences move while the second ones stand still, the signature of a parabola; the constant second difference is twice the leading coefficient times the squared spacing.

$$y=x^{2}+1$$

tasks.title: A Stretched Parabola and Its Turning Point
tasks.context: Let $p(x)=3x^{2}-12x+7$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The axis of symmetry of $p$ is the line $x=2$.
The vertex of the graph of $p$ is the point $\left(2,-5\right)$.
The smallest value taken by $p$ is $7$.
The leading coefficient of $p$ is $3$.
$p$ is decreasing for every $x<2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A parabola is its own mirror image in one vertical line, and the abscissa of that line is settled by the first two coefficients alone.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$p(x)=3x^{2}-12x+7$$

$$x=-\frac{-12}{2\cdot 3}=2$$

The mirror line is $x=2$, exactly the line named in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The turning point lies on the axis of symmetry, so its abscissa comes from the coefficients and its height is the value of the function there.

$$p(x)=3x^{2}-12x+7$$

$$x=-\frac{-12}{2\cdot 3}=2$$

Evaluating on the axis gives the height.

$$p(2)=3\cdot 2^{2}-12\cdot 2+7=-5$$

The turning point is $\left(2,-5\right)$, the point the claim names, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

A parabola reaches its extreme value at the turning point and nowhere else, so locate the axis first and then read the height there.

$$p(x)=3x^{2}-12x+7$$

$$x=-\frac{-12}{2\cdot 3}=2$$

$$p(2)=3\cdot 2^{2}-12\cdot 2+7=-5$$

The leading coefficient $3$ is positive, so the arms rise on both sides and $-5$ is the smallest value the function ever takes; there is no largest one.

The smallest value is $-5$ while the claim reports $7$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The leading coefficient is the number multiplying $x^{2}$ once every bracket has been multiplied out, and any minus sign in front belongs to it.

$$p(x)=3x^{2}-12x+7$$

$$a=3$$

Its sign tells the opening direction and its size tells how narrow the parabola is.

The leading coefficient is $3$, the number the claim gives, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

A parabola changes direction exactly once, at its axis, so a claim about a whole half-line is decided by where that axis sits.

$$p(x)=3x^{2}-12x+7$$

$$x=-\frac{-12}{2\cdot 3}=2$$

With a positive leading coefficient the graph falls on everything to the left of $x=2$ and rises on everything to its right.

The half-line $x<2$ lies entirely on the decreasing side of the axis, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
A single quadratic rule carries every claim.

$$p(x)=3x^{2}-12x+7$$

Two standard readings cover most of what follows: the vertex from the completed square, and the sum and product of the roots from the coefficients.

$$\text{vertex}=\left(2,-5\right)\qquad S=4\qquad P=\frac{7}{3}$$

A positive discriminant puts two crossings on the $x$-axis.

$$\Delta=60$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-5$.

tasks.title: Ticket Price Against Weekly Revenue
tasks.context: A small cinema models its weekly revenue in euros at a ticket price of $x$ euros by $R(x)=-2x^{2}+36x$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The weekly revenue is largest at $x=9$.
The largest possible weekly revenue equals $162$ euros.
The weekly revenue is zero exactly at $x=0$ and $x=18$.
Between $x=2$ and $x=6$ the weekly revenue changes at an average rate of $16$ euros per unit of $x$.
At $x=10$ the weekly revenue equals $160$ euros.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The weekly revenue follows a parabola, and a parabola turns exactly once: the best input is the abscissa of the turning point.

$$R(x)=-2x^{2}+36x$$

$$x=-\frac{36}{2\cdot \left(-2\right)}=9$$

The leading coefficient $-2$ is negative, so the model rises to that input and falls afterwards.

The weekly revenue is therefore largest at $x=9$, the input in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The extreme weekly revenue is the height of the turning point, so find the input that produces it and evaluate the model there.

$$x=-\frac{36}{2\cdot \left(-2\right)}=9$$

$$R(9)=-2\cdot 9^{2}+36\cdot 9=162$$

Because the leading coefficient $-2$ is negative, this height is the largest value the model ever reaches.

The extreme weekly revenue is $162$, the figure the claim gives, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The weekly revenue vanishes where the model takes the value zero, so solve that quadratic equation.

$$R(x)=0$$

$$-2x^{2}+36x=0$$

$$x_{1}=0\qquad x_{2}=18$$

The weekly revenue is zero exactly at those two inputs, as claimed, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

An average rate compares the change of the weekly revenue with the change of the input, so both endpoint values are needed first.

$$R(2)=-2\cdot 2^{2}+36\cdot 2=64$$

$$R(6)=-2\cdot 6^{2}+36\cdot 6=144$$

$$\frac{R\left(6\right)-R\left(2\right)}{6-2}=\frac{80}{4}=20$$

The average rate over that stretch is $20$, not $16$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The model turns any input into the weekly revenue, so a claim about one particular input is settled by a single substitution.

$$R(x)=-2x^{2}+36x$$

$$R(10)=-2\cdot 10^{2}+36\cdot 10=160$$

The model returns $160$ there, the figure named in the claim, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The story reduces to one formula and the quantities it links.

$$R(x)=-2x^{2}+36x$$

The axis formula fixes the turning point, while the sum $S$ and the product $P$ of the roots come out of the coefficients with no equation to solve.

$$\text{vertex}=\left(9,162\right)\qquad S=18\qquad P=0$$

A positive discriminant puts two crossings on the $x$-axis, placed symmetrically around the axis of the parabola.

$$\Delta=1296\qquad x_{1}=0\qquad x_{2}=18$$

The arms open downwards, so the turning point is the highest point of the graph and the largest value is $162$.

tasks.title: Completing the Square With a Negative Constant
tasks.context: Consider the parabola $q(x)=x^{2}+8x+10$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Completing the square gives $q(x)=\left(x+4\right)^{2}-6$.
The vertex of the graph of $q$ is the point $\left(-4,-6\right)$.
The smallest value taken by $q$ is $10$.
$q(x)\ge -6$ holds for every real $x$.
The axis of symmetry of $q$ is the line $x=4$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Completing the square rewrites a parabola as $a(x-h)^{2}+k$, where $h$ is the abscissa of the axis and $k$ the height of the turning point, so both numbers have to be produced first.

$$q(x)=x^{2}+8x+10$$

$$x=-\frac{8}{2\cdot 1}=-4$$

The height of the turning point is the value on that axis.

$$q\left(-4\right)=\left(-4\right)^{2}+8\cdot \left(-4\right)+10=-6$$

Putting the stretch, the shift and the height together gives

$$q(x)=\left(x+4\right)^{2}-6$$

This is the very expression the claim displays, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The turning point lies on the axis of symmetry, so its abscissa comes from the coefficients and its height is the value of the function there.

$$q(x)=x^{2}+8x+10$$

$$x=-\frac{8}{2\cdot 1}=-4$$

Evaluating on the axis gives the height.

$$q\left(-4\right)=\left(-4\right)^{2}+8\cdot \left(-4\right)+10=-6$$

The turning point is $\left(-4,-6\right)$, the point the claim names, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

A parabola reaches its extreme value at the turning point and nowhere else, so locate the axis first and then read the height there.

$$q(x)=x^{2}+8x+10$$

$$x=-\frac{8}{2\cdot 1}=-4$$

$$q\left(-4\right)=\left(-4\right)^{2}+8\cdot \left(-4\right)+10=-6$$

The leading coefficient $1$ is positive, so the arms rise on both sides and $-6$ is the smallest value the function ever takes; there is no largest one.

The smallest value is $-6$ while the claim reports $10$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

An inequality that has to hold for every real $x$ is a statement about the extreme value of the parabola, so the turning point decides it.

$$x=-\frac{8}{2\cdot 1}=-4$$

$$q\left(-4\right)=\left(-4\right)^{2}+8\cdot \left(-4\right)+10=-6$$

The leading coefficient $1$ is positive, so the values never drop below $-6$.

$$q(x)\ge -6$$

The bound $-6$ is reached once and never passed anywhere else, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

A parabola is its own mirror image in one vertical line, and the abscissa of that line is settled by the first two coefficients alone.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$q(x)=x^{2}+8x+10$$

$$x=-\frac{8}{2\cdot 1}=-4$$

The mirror line is $x=-4$ while the claim names $x=4$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Everything below refers to the same parabola.

$$q(x)=x^{2}+8x+10$$

Before testing anything, it pays to write down the vertex together with the sum and the product of the roots, all three being coefficient arithmetic.

$$\text{vertex}=\left(-4,-6\right)\qquad S=-8\qquad P=10$$

A positive discriminant puts two crossings on the $x$-axis.

$$\Delta=24$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-6$.

tasks.title: Which Model Fits the Measurements?
tasks.context: A meter reading was recorded once per minute for five minutes; $x$ counts the minutes and $y$ is the reading. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The table is consistent with a linear model.
A linear rule through the table has slope $-3$.
The average rate of change between $x=0$ and $x=4$ is $-3$.
The table is produced by the rule $y=-3x+10$.
The second differences of the $y$-values are constant and equal to $-3$.

**A.** → True

A table is consistent with a line when its first differences are constant, and with a parabola when the second differences are constant while the first ones are not.

$$\text{first differences}:\ -3,\ -3,\ -3,\ -3$$

$$\text{second differences}:\ 0,\ 0,\ 0$$

$$y=-3x+10$$

The pattern is exactly the one a linear rule produces, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The slope of a line through a table is the change of the output divided by the change of the input, which is the same for every pair of rows only when the first differences are constant.

$$\text{first differences}:\ -3,\ -3,\ -3,\ -3$$

$$m=\frac{-3}{1}=-3$$

The line through the table has slope $-3$, as claimed, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

An average rate of change over a stretch is read from the two end rows only: the change of the output divided by the change of the input.

$$y\left(0\right)=10\qquad y\left(4\right)=-2$$

$$\frac{-2-10}{4-0}=\frac{-12}{4}=-3$$

The average rate over that stretch is $-3$, the figure claimed, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Testing a proposed rule against a table is a matter of substitution: the rule has to reproduce every row, and for a rule of degree at most two three rows already pin it down.

$$y=-3x+10$$

Running the claimed rule over the first rows gives

$$0\mapsto 10,\quad 1\mapsto 7,\quad 2\mapsto 4$$

Every row comes out right, which identifies the claimed rule as the one behind the table, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Differencing twice is the standard test for a parabola: the second differences of a quadratic rule are constant, and they are zero for a line.

$$\text{first differences}:\ -3,\ -3,\ -3,\ -3$$

$$\text{second differences}:\ 0,\ 0,\ 0$$

They are all equal to $0$ while the claim names $-3$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The table is the whole stem, so read it as a list of pairs.

$$\left(0,10\right),\ \left(1,7\right),\ \left(2,4\right),\ \left(3,1\right),\ \left(4,-2\right)$$

The inputs are equally spaced, which makes the differences of neighbouring outputs the fastest diagnostic tool available.

$$\text{first}:\ -3,\ -3,\ -3,\ -3\qquad \text{second}:\ 0,\ 0,\ 0$$

Constant first differences mean a line, and the slope is one difference divided by the spacing of the inputs.

$$y=-3x+10$$

tasks.title: A Negative Stretch Keeps the Zeros
tasks.context: Let $p(x)=-3\left(x+2\right)\left(x-5\right)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The roots of $p$ are $-2$ and $5$.
The graph of $p$ opens downwards.
The axis of symmetry of $p$ is the line $x=\frac{3}{2}$.
The leading coefficient of $p$ is $3$.
The two roots of $p$ multiply to $-10$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The roots are the inputs where the graph touches the $x$-axis, so set the rule equal to zero; the discriminant says first how many such inputs exist.

$$p(x)=-3x^{2}+9x+30$$

$$\Delta=9^{2}-4\left(-3\right)\left(30\right)=441$$

A positive discriminant gives two separate roots, delivered by the quadratic formula.

$$x_{1}=-2\qquad x_{2}=5$$

The zeros are $-2$ and $5$, the pair named in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Far away from the turning point the square term dwarfs the rest, so the sign of the leading coefficient decides on its own which way the arms point.

$$p(x)=-3x^{2}+9x+30$$

$$a=-3$$

A negative leading coefficient sends both arms downwards, and the turning point is the highest point of the graph.

The graph opens downwards, which is what the claim says, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

A parabola is its own mirror image in one vertical line, and the abscissa of that line is settled by the first two coefficients alone.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$p(x)=-3x^{2}+9x+30$$

$$x=-\frac{9}{2\cdot \left(-3\right)}=\frac{3}{2}$$

The mirror line is $x=\frac{3}{2}$, exactly the line named in the claim, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The leading coefficient is the number multiplying $x^{2}$ once every bracket has been multiplied out, and any minus sign in front belongs to it.

$$p(x)=-3x^{2}+9x+30$$

$$a=-3$$

Its sign tells the opening direction and its size tells how narrow the parabola is.

The leading coefficient is $-3$, not $3$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The second of Vieta's relations gives the product of the roots as the constant term divided by the leading coefficient.

$$P=\frac{c}{a}$$

$$p(x)=-3x^{2}+9x+30$$

$$P=\frac{30}{-3}=-10$$

Multiplying the roots $-2$ and $5$ confirms the value.

The product is $-10$, exactly what the claim reports, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Only one parabola is in play here.

$$p(x)=-3\left(x+2\right)\left(x-5\right)$$

Multiplying out puts the same rule in standard form, where every coefficient can be read off directly.

$$p(x)=-3x^{2}+9x+30$$

Completing the square locates the turning point, and Vieta's relations give the sum $S$ and the product $P$ of the roots without solving anything.

$$\text{vertex}=\left(\frac{3}{2},\frac{147}{4}\right)\qquad S=3\qquad P=-10$$

Because the discriminant is positive the parabola meets the $x$-axis in two points, and factoring recovers them.

$$\Delta=441\qquad x_{1}=-2\qquad x_{2}=5$$

The arms open downwards, so the turning point is the highest point of the graph and the largest value is $\frac{147}{4}$.

tasks.title: A Parabola With the $y$-Axis as Its Mirror
tasks.context: The parabola $p$ has the rule $p(x)=2x^{2}-18$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graph of $p$ is symmetric about the $y$-axis.
The values $p(-3)$ and $p(3)$ are equal.
The roots of $p$ are $3$ and $-3$.
The two roots of $p$ multiply to $9$.
The smallest value taken by $p$ is $-18$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Symmetry about the $y$-axis means the axis of symmetry is the line $x=0$, and that happens exactly when the middle coefficient disappears.

$$p(x)=2x^{2}-18$$

$$x=-\frac{0}{2\cdot 2}=0$$

Testing a pair of opposite inputs shows the same behaviour from the other side.

$$p(-x)=2x^{2}-18$$

The rule is unchanged when $x$ is replaced by $-x$, the algebraic form of symmetry about the $y$-axis, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Two inputs give the same output exactly when they lie at the same distance from the axis of symmetry, but the safest check is to work both values out.

$$x=-\frac{0}{2\cdot 2}=0$$

$$p\left(-3\right)=2\cdot \left(-3\right)^{2}-18=0$$

$$p(3)=2\cdot 3^{2}-18=0$$

The midpoint of $-3$ and $3$ is $0$, which is the axis itself.

Both inputs return $0$, an equal pair of values, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The roots are the inputs where the graph touches the $x$-axis, so set the rule equal to zero; the discriminant says first how many such inputs exist.

$$p(x)=2x^{2}-18$$

$$\Delta=0^{2}-4\left(2\right)\left(-18\right)=144$$

A positive discriminant gives two separate roots, delivered by the quadratic formula.

$$x_{1}=-3\qquad x_{2}=3$$

The zeros are $-3$ and $3$, the pair named in the claim, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The second of Vieta's relations gives the product of the roots as the constant term divided by the leading coefficient.

$$P=\frac{c}{a}$$

$$p(x)=2x^{2}-18$$

$$P=\frac{-18}{2}=-9$$

Multiplying the roots $-3$ and $3$ confirms the value.

The product is $-9$ while the claim reports $9$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

A parabola reaches its extreme value at the turning point and nowhere else, so locate the axis first and then read the height there.

$$p(x)=2x^{2}-18$$

$$x=-\frac{0}{2\cdot 2}=0$$

$$p(0)=2\cdot 0^{2}-18=-18$$

The leading coefficient $2$ is positive, so the arms rise on both sides and $-18$ is the smallest value the function ever takes; there is no largest one.

That extreme value is $-18$, exactly as claimed, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
A single quadratic rule carries every claim.

$$p(x)=2x^{2}-18$$

Two standard readings cover most of what follows: the vertex from the completed square, and the sum and product of the roots from the coefficients.

$$\text{vertex}=\left(0,-18\right)\qquad S=0\qquad P=-9$$

A positive discriminant puts two crossings on the $x$-axis, placed symmetrically around the axis of the parabola.

$$\Delta=144\qquad x_{1}=-3\qquad x_{2}=3$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-18$.

tasks.title: Rebuilding a Parabola From Its Zeros
tasks.context: A parabola $p$ has zeros $-4$ and $2$ and leading coefficient $3$; recover its rule before judging the claims. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The rule is $p(x)=3x^{2}+6x-24$.
The axis of symmetry of $p$ is the line $x=-1$.
The graph of $p$ meets the $y$-axis at $y=-24$.
The smallest value taken by $p$ is $-27$.
The two roots of $p$ add up to $4$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Two zeros and a leading coefficient describe a parabola completely: the zeros fix the factors and the coefficient fixes the vertical stretch.

$$p(x)=3\left(x+4\right)\left(x-2\right)$$

Multiplying the two brackets out puts the rule in standard form.

$$p(x)=3x^{2}+6x-24$$

The rebuilt rule is the one printed in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A parabola is its own mirror image in one vertical line, and the abscissa of that line is settled by the first two coefficients alone.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$p(x)=3x^{2}+6x-24$$

$$x=-\frac{6}{2\cdot 3}=-1$$

The mirror line is $x=-1$, exactly the line named in the claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The graph meets the $y$-axis where the input is zero, so the intercept is simply the constant term of the rule.

$$p(x)=3x^{2}+6x-24$$

$$p(0)=3\cdot 0^{2}+6\cdot 0-24=-24$$

The graph cuts the $y$-axis at $y=-24$, the height the claim names, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

A parabola reaches its extreme value at the turning point and nowhere else, so locate the axis first and then read the height there.

$$p(x)=3x^{2}+6x-24$$

$$x=-\frac{6}{2\cdot 3}=-1$$

$$p\left(-1\right)=3\cdot \left(-1\right)^{2}+6\cdot \left(-1\right)-24=-27$$

The leading coefficient $3$ is positive, so the arms rise on both sides and $-27$ is the smallest value the function ever takes; there is no largest one.

That extreme value is $-27$, exactly as claimed, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Vieta's relations read the sum of the two roots straight off the coefficients, with no equation to solve: it is minus the middle coefficient divided by the leading one.

$$S=-\frac{b}{a}$$

$$p(x)=3x^{2}+6x-24$$

$$S=-\frac{6}{3}=-2$$

The roots themselves are $-4$ and $2$, and they do add up to $-2$.

The sum is $-2$ while the claim reports $4$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Two zeros and a leading coefficient describe a parabola completely: the zeros fix the factors and the coefficient fixes the vertical stretch.

$$p(x)=3\left(x+4\right)\left(x-2\right)$$

Multiplying the two brackets out puts the rule in standard form.

$$p(x)=3x^{2}+6x-24$$

The axis formula fixes the turning point, while the sum $S$ and the product $P$ of the roots come out of the coefficients with no equation to solve.

$$\text{vertex}=\left(-1,-27\right)\qquad S=-2\qquad P=-8$$

The discriminant comes out positive, so the graph cuts the $x$-axis twice, once on either side of the axis of symmetry.

$$\Delta=324\qquad x_{1}=-4\qquad x_{2}=2$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-27$.

tasks.title: A Line Fixed by a Slope and One Point
tasks.context: A line $u$ has slope $-\frac{1}{2}$ and passes through the point $(4,1)$; recover its rule before judging the claims. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The rule is $u(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x+3$.
The graph of $u$ meets the $y$-axis at $y=3$.
The graph of $u$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x=6$.
$u$ is increasing.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A slope and one point are enough for a line: start at the given point and walk along the slope.

$$u(x)=-\frac{1}{2}\left(x-4\right)+1$$

Expanding the bracket puts the rule in the familiar shape.

$$u(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x+3$$

The rebuilt rule is the one printed in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The graph meets the $y$-axis where the input is zero, so the intercept is simply the constant term of the rule.

$$u(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x+3$$

$$u(0)=-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 0+3=3$$

The graph cuts the $y$-axis at $y=3$, the height the claim names, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The graph crosses the $x$-axis where the height is zero, so set the rule equal to zero and solve the linear equation.

$$-\frac{1}{2}x+3=0$$

$$-\frac{1}{2}x=-3$$

$$x=\left(-3\right)\cdot \left(-2\right)=6$$

The crossing is at $x=6$, exactly where the claim puts it, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Evaluating a function means putting the number in place of every $x$ and working the arithmetic out once.

$$u(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x+3$$

$$u\left(-2\right)=-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \left(-2\right)+3=4$$

The graph therefore passes through the point $\left(-2,4\right)$.

The value is $4$, precisely the number in the claim, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

A line has the same steepness everywhere, so its direction is decided once and for all by the sign of the slope.

$$u(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x+3$$

$$m=-\frac{1}{2}$$

Because the slope is negative, every step to the right lowers the height.

The function is decreasing, not increasing, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
A slope and one point are enough for a line: start at the given point and walk along the slope.

$$u(x)=-\frac{1}{2}\left(x-4\right)+1$$

Expanding the bracket puts the rule in the familiar shape.

$$u(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x+3$$

Two numbers describe it completely: the slope, which is the change of height per unit step, and the height above the origin.

$$m=-\frac{1}{2}\qquad u(0)=3$$

Setting the height to zero locates the single crossing of the $x$-axis, and the sign of the slope fixes the direction once and for all.

$$-\frac{1}{2}x+3=0\Rightarrow x=6$$

tasks.title: Who Wins Far to the Right?
tasks.context: Let $f$ be a non-constant linear function and let $g$ be a quadratic function whose leading coefficient $a$ is nonzero. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $a$ is positive, then $g(x)>f(x)$ for all sufficiently large $x$.
If $a$ is positive, then $g(x)>f(x)$ for every real $x$.
If $a$ is negative, then $g(x)<f(x)$ for all sufficiently large $x$.
There is a line whose graph stays above the whole graph of an upward-opening parabola.
If $g$ opens upwards, then the difference $g-f$ is bounded below on $\mathbb{R}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Far out to the right the contest between a line and a parabola is settled by the square term alone, so write $f(x)=mx+q$ and compare the two functions through their difference.

$$g(x)-f(x)=ax^{2}+\left(b-m\right)x+\left(c-q\right)$$

Subtracting a line never touches the coefficient of $x^{2}$, so the difference is again a parabola with leading coefficient $a>0$: it opens upwards and takes negative values at most on the bounded interval between its two roots.

$$g(x)-f(x)=a\left(x-h\right)^{2}+k\quad\text{with }a>0$$

Once $x$ lies to the right of that interval the difference is strictly positive and grows without bound, since the square term outruns the linear and constant ones.

The parabola therefore overtakes the line and stays above it for all sufficiently large $x$, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Winning the race far to the right says nothing about the region near the origin, where the linear term can still be in front, so a single well-chosen pair settles the claim.

$$g(x)=x^{2}\qquad f(x)=x$$

Here $a=1>0$ and the line is non-constant, so both hypotheses hold. Test the two functions halfway between the points where they agree.

$$g\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{4}\qquad f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{2}$$

At that abscissa the line is the higher of the two, and indeed the difference $g(x)-f(x)=x^{2}-x=x(x-1)$ is negative on the whole interval between $0$ and $1$.

An upward-opening parabola can dip below a line on a bounded stretch, so the inequality cannot hold for every real $x$, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The same comparison works upside down: subtracting the line leaves the coefficient of $x^{2}$ untouched, and now that coefficient is negative.

$$g(x)-f(x)=ax^{2}+\left(b-m\right)x+\left(c-q\right),\quad a<0$$

A downward-opening parabola is positive at most between its two roots, so beyond the larger of them the difference stays strictly negative and falls without bound.

$$x\text{ large}\implies g(x)-f(x)<0\implies g(x)<f(x)$$

Far enough to the right the line is above the parabola, exactly as the claim says, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A line staying above the whole graph would mean the difference $g-f$ never becomes positive, so look at what that difference actually does.

$$g(x)-f(x)=ax^{2}+\left(b-m\right)x+\left(c-q\right),\quad a>0$$

Being an upward-opening parabola, this difference grows beyond every bound as $x$ increases; for instance with $g(x)=x^{2}$ and any line $f(x)=mx+q$ the difference is positive as soon as $x>m+|q|+1$.

$$x^{2}-mx-q>0\text{ for all large }x$$

Every line is eventually overtaken, so no line can stay above an upward-opening parabola everywhere, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Bounded below means the values never sink past some fixed level, and for a parabola that level is supplied by the vertex.

$$d(x)=g(x)-f(x)=ax^{2}+\left(b-m\right)x+\left(c-q\right),\quad a>0$$

Completing the square isolates a non-negative square multiplied by the positive number $a$, so the whole expression can never drop below the constant left over.

$$d(x)=a\left(x-h\right)^{2}+k\ge k\quad\text{for every real }x$$

The number $k$ is the height of the vertex of $d$, and it depends only on the coefficients, not on where $x$ happens to be.

The difference has a genuine smallest value and is therefore bounded below on all of $\mathbb{R}$, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
No numbers are on offer, so the meetings of the graphs have to be counted through the difference $g-f$ in general form.

$$g(x)-f(x)=0$$

Common points of a line and a parabola solve a single quadratic equation, so there can never be more than two of them. Far out on either side the $x^{2}$ term outgrows every linear term, so the parabola decides who ends up on top.

tasks.title: When Is the Difference Still Curved?
tasks.context: Let $f$ be a linear function, let $g$ be a quadratic function whose leading coefficient $a$ is nonzero, and set $d=g-f$. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The coefficient of $x^{2}$ in $d$ is nonzero.
Some choice of $f$ makes $d$ a linear function.
Some choice of $f$ makes the coefficient of $x$ in $d$ vanish.
If the coefficient of $x$ in $d$ vanishes, then the axis of $g$ is the vertical coordinate axis.
Whatever $f$ is, the graph of $d$ opens in the same direction as the graph of $g$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Only the parabola can contribute a square term, so expand the difference and watch which coefficient the line is able to reach.

$$d(x)=\left(ax^{2}+bx+c\right)-\left(mx+q\right)$$

$$d(x)=ax^{2}+\left(b-m\right)x+\left(c-q\right)$$

The line only ever touches the $x$ term and the constant term; the coefficient in front of $x^{2}$ is copied straight from $g$, and it is non-zero because $g$ is a parabola.

That coefficient equals $a\neq 0$ whatever $f$ is, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Making $d$ a line would require the square term to disappear, so ask which choice of $f$ could cancel it.

$$d(x)=ax^{2}+\left(b-m\right)x+\left(c-q\right)$$

A line has no $x^{2}$ term at all, so subtracting it leaves $a$ in place; the only way to reach a zero coefficient would be $a=0$, which is excluded by hypothesis.

$$a\neq 0\implies d\text{ still has a square term}$$

No choice of $f$ can flatten the difference into a line, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The coefficient of $x$ in the difference is the gap between the middle coefficient of $g$ and the slope of $f$, so it can be steered by choosing the slope.

$$d(x)=ax^{2}+\left(b-m\right)x+\left(c-q\right)$$

Setting $m=b$ makes that gap vanish, and such a line certainly exists: take $f(x)=bx$, for example.

$$m=b\implies d(x)=ax^{2}+\left(c-q\right)$$

One suitable line removes the $x$ term completely, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A vanishing $x$ term in $d$ means $m=b$, and that condition concerns the difference, not the original parabola.

$$b-m=0\implies d(x)=ax^{2}+\left(c-q\right)$$

The axis of $d$ is then the vertical line through the origin, but the axis of $g$ is still computed from the coefficients of $g$ alone.

$$g(x)=x^{2}+2x,\quad f(x)=2x\implies d(x)=x^{2}$$

Here the $x$ term of $d$ has indeed vanished, yet the axis of $g$ is the line $x=-1$ and not the vertical coordinate axis.

The condition on $d$ says nothing about where the axis of $g$ sits, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The opening direction of a parabola is read off from the sign of its coefficient of $x^{2}$, so compare that single number for $g$ and for $d$.

$$d(x)=ax^{2}+\left(b-m\right)x+\left(c-q\right)$$

Subtracting a line changes the $x$ term and the constant term only, so both graphs carry the very same leading coefficient $a$.

$$a>0\implies\text{both open upwards}\qquad a<0\implies\text{both open downwards}$$

The two parabolas always turn the same way, whichever line is subtracted, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
No coefficients are fixed, so the letters $a$, $b$ and $c$ have to be handled through the formulas that hold for every parabola.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

The axis of symmetry sits at $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$, so it follows the first two coefficients and ignores the constant term entirely.

The difference of the two functions is given its own name, so watch which of its coefficients still depend on the line.

tasks.title: Touching at the Vertex
tasks.context: Let $f(x)=2$ and $g(x)=x^{2}+2x+3$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graphs of $f$ and $g$ have exactly one point in common.
That common point is the vertex of the graph of $g$.
At the common point the two graphs have the same slope.
The two graphs cross each other at that point.
The function $g$ has two distinct real roots.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Common points are the solutions of $g(x)=f(x)$, so bring everything to one side and see what kind of expression appears.

$$x^{2}+2x+3-2=x^{2}+2x+1=0$$

The left-hand side is a perfect square, which can vanish only where the bracket itself does.

$$\left(x+1\right)^{2}=0\iff x=-1$$

A double root counts as a single point of the plane, namely $(-1,2)$, and there is nowhere else the two graphs can agree.

Exactly one point is shared, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The vertex sits on the axis of symmetry, whose abscissa comes from the first two coefficients, and its height is the value of $g$ there.

$$x=-\frac{2}{2\cdot 1}=-1$$

$$g(-1)=1-2+3=2$$

So the vertex is the point $(-1,2)$, which is exactly the abscissa and height found for the single common point.

$$f(-1)=2=g(-1)$$

The contact happens precisely at the vertex, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The line is horizontal, so its slope is zero; compare that with the slope of the parabola at the contact abscissa.

$$g'(x)=2x+2$$

$$g'(-1)=-2+2=0$$

Both slopes are zero at $x=-1$, which is no accident: the tangent at a vertex is always horizontal, and the difference $\left(x+1\right)^{2}$ having a double root is the algebraic form of that agreement.

The two graphs share the same slope where they touch, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Crossing would mean the difference changes sign at the contact point, so track the sign of that difference.

$$g(x)-f(x)=\left(x+1\right)^{2}$$

A square is never negative, and here it is strictly positive on both sides of $x=-1$.

$$g(-2)-f(-2)=1>0\qquad g(0)-f(0)=1>0$$

The parabola stays above the line on either side and merely comes down to touch it once, so the line never passes from one side of the curve to the other.

The graphs touch without crossing, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Real roots of $g$ exist according to the sign of its discriminant, so compute that number.

$$\Delta=2^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 3=4-12=-8$$

A negative discriminant leaves no real square root in the quadratic formula, so the equation $g(x)=0$ has no real solution at all.

$$g(x)=\left(x+1\right)^{2}+2\ge 2>0$$

Vertex form says the same thing more directly: the lowest value of $g$ is $2$, so the graph stays entirely above the horizontal axis.

There are no real roots, let alone two distinct ones, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Both rules are handed over with numbers already in place:

$$f(x)=2\qquad g(x)=x^{2} + 2 x + 3$$

No work beyond reading is needed for the slope, for the two values at $0$ and for the opening direction, which is upwards here because of the sign in front of $x^{2}$.

$$m=0\qquad f(0)=2\qquad g(0)=3\qquad a=1$$

Since the parabola is concrete, the vertex can be computed once and reused: the axis first, then the height above it.

$$g(x)=\left(x+1\right)^{2}+2\qquad \text{vertex}=\left(-1,2\right)$$

Vieta's relations read the sum $S$ and the product $P$ of the roots of $g$ straight off the coefficients, and the discriminant of $g$ says how many real roots there are to sum in the first place.

$$S=-2\qquad P=3\qquad \Delta_{g}=-8$$

Common points are the roots of $f-g$, and that difference is again a quadratic, so its discriminant settles the count: one here.

$$f(x)-g(x)=- x^{2} - 2 x - 1\qquad \Delta=0$$

tasks.title: The Quadratic Hidden Behind a Data Table
tasks.context: The five pairs below come from one polynomial rule of degree at most two. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The first differences of the $y$-values are constant.
The second differences of the $y$-values are constant and equal to $4$.
A quadratic rule through the table has leading coefficient $2$.
The table is produced by the rule $y=2x^{2}-3x+1$.
The $y$-values in the table are smallest at $x=1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

With equally spaced inputs the differences of neighbouring outputs do all the work: constant first differences are the fingerprint of a line.

$$y:\ 1,\ 0,\ 3,\ 10,\ 21$$

$$\text{first differences}:\ -1,\ 3,\ 7,\ 11$$

The steps come in different sizes, which is exactly what non-constant first differences mean, so the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Differencing twice is the standard test for a parabola: the second differences of a quadratic rule are constant, and they are zero for a line.

$$\text{first differences}:\ -1,\ 3,\ 7,\ 11$$

$$\text{second differences}:\ 4,\ 4,\ 4$$

They are all equal to $4$, the value the claim names, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

For equally spaced inputs the constant second difference of a quadratic rule equals twice the leading coefficient times the square of the spacing, so the coefficient can be read off the table directly.

$$\text{second difference}=2a\left(\Delta x\right)^{2}$$

$$\text{second differences}:\ 4,\ 4,\ 4$$

$$a=\frac{4}{2\cdot 1^{2}}=2$$

The leading coefficient is $2$, the number the claim gives, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Testing a proposed rule against a table is a matter of substitution: the rule has to reproduce every row, and for a rule of degree at most two three rows already pin it down.

$$y=2x^{2}-3x+1$$

Running the claimed rule over the first rows gives

$$0\mapsto 1,\quad 1\mapsto 0,\quad 2\mapsto 3$$

Every row comes out right, which identifies the claimed rule as the one behind the table, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

A claim about the rows of the table is settled inside the table itself: compare the listed outputs and see where the extreme one sits.

$$y:\ 1,\ 0,\ 3,\ 10,\ 21$$

$$\text{smallest listed value}=0$$

That value appears at $x=1$.

The smallest entry of the table does sit at $x=1$, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The table is the whole stem, so read it as a list of pairs.

$$\left(0,1\right),\ \left(1,0\right),\ \left(2,3\right),\ \left(3,10\right),\ \left(4,21\right)$$

The inputs are equally spaced, which makes the differences of neighbouring outputs the fastest diagnostic tool available.

$$\text{first}:\ -1,\ 3,\ 7,\ 11\qquad \text{second}:\ 4,\ 4,\ 4$$

The first differences move while the second ones stand still, the signature of a parabola; the constant second difference is twice the leading coefficient times the squared spacing.

$$y=2x^{2}-3x+1$$

tasks.title: Turning Point, Zeros and a Horizontal Probe
tasks.context: Let $q(x)=x^{2}-10x+21$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The vertex of the graph of $q$ is the point $\left(5,-4\right)$.
The roots of $q$ are $3$ and $7$.
The distance between the two roots of $q$ is $4$.
The smallest value taken by $q$ is $21$.
The horizontal line $y=-4$ meets the graph of $q$ at two different points.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The turning point lies on the axis of symmetry, so its abscissa comes from the coefficients and its height is the value of the function there.

$$q(x)=x^{2}-10x+21$$

$$x=-\frac{-10}{2\cdot 1}=5$$

Evaluating on the axis gives the height.

$$q(5)=5^{2}-10\cdot 5+21=-4$$

The turning point is $\left(5,-4\right)$, the point the claim names, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The roots are the inputs where the graph touches the $x$-axis, so set the rule equal to zero; the discriminant says first how many such inputs exist.

$$q(x)=x^{2}-10x+21$$

$$\Delta=\left(-10\right)^{2}-4\left(1\right)\left(21\right)=16$$

A positive discriminant gives two separate roots, delivered by the quadratic formula.

$$x_{1}=3\qquad x_{2}=7$$

The zeros are $3$ and $7$, the pair named in the claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The two roots sit symmetrically on either side of the axis, so their gap is the square root of the discriminant divided by the size of the leading coefficient.

$$\left|x_{1}-x_{2}\right|=\frac{\sqrt{\Delta}}{\left|a\right|}$$

$$\Delta=\left(-10\right)^{2}-4\left(1\right)\left(21\right)=16$$

$$\left|x_{1}-x_{2}\right|=\frac{4}{1}=4$$

The roots $3$ and $7$ are indeed $4$ apart.

The gap is $4$, the distance the claim reports, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A parabola reaches its extreme value at the turning point and nowhere else, so locate the axis first and then read the height there.

$$q(x)=x^{2}-10x+21$$

$$x=-\frac{-10}{2\cdot 1}=5$$

$$q(5)=5^{2}-10\cdot 5+21=-4$$

The leading coefficient $1$ is positive, so the arms rise on both sides and $-4$ is the smallest value the function ever takes; there is no largest one.

The smallest value is $-4$ while the claim reports $21$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

A horizontal line meets the parabola where the rule takes that constant value, so move the constant to the other side and count the solutions of the quadratic that is left.

$$q(x)+4=x^{2}-10x+25$$

$$\Delta=\left(-10\right)^{2}-4\left(1\right)\left(25\right)=0$$

The turning point sits at height $-4$ and the arms open upwards, so the levels the graph reaches twice are exactly those above $-4$.

The level $y=-4$ is the height of the turning point itself, where the line touches the graph once instead of cutting it twice, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Everything below refers to the same parabola.

$$q(x)=x^{2}-10x+21$$

Before testing anything, it pays to write down the vertex together with the sum and the product of the roots, all three being coefficient arithmetic.

$$\text{vertex}=\left(5,-4\right)\qquad S=10\qquad P=21$$

Because the discriminant is positive the parabola meets the $x$-axis in two points, and factoring recovers them.

$$\Delta=16\qquad x_{1}=3\qquad x_{2}=7$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-4$.

tasks.title: Fuel Use Against Cruising Speed
tasks.context: For a lorry cruising at $x$ kilometres per hour, the fuel used on a fixed route is modelled by $F(x)=\frac{1}{50}x^{2}-2x+80$ litres. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The fuel use is smallest at $x=50$.
The smallest possible fuel use equals $30$ litres.
Between $x=20$ and $x=40$ the fuel use changes at an average rate of $-1$ litres per unit of $x$.
The fuel use is never zero.
At $x=100$ the fuel use equals $80$ litres.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The fuel use follows a parabola, and a parabola turns exactly once: the best input is the abscissa of the turning point.

$$F(x)=\frac{1}{50}x^{2}-2x+80$$

$$x=-\frac{-2}{2\cdot \left(\frac{1}{50}\right)}=50$$

The leading coefficient $\frac{1}{50}$ is positive, so the model falls to that input and rises afterwards.

The fuel use is therefore smallest at $x=50$, the input in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The extreme fuel use is the height of the turning point, so find the input that produces it and evaluate the model there.

$$x=-\frac{-2}{2\cdot \left(\frac{1}{50}\right)}=50$$

$$F(50)=\frac{1}{50}\cdot 50^{2}-2\cdot 50+80=30$$

Because the leading coefficient $\frac{1}{50}$ is positive, this height is the smallest value the model ever reaches.

The extreme fuel use is $30$, the figure the claim gives, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

An average rate compares the change of the fuel use with the change of the input, so both endpoint values are needed first.

$$F(20)=\frac{1}{50}\cdot 20^{2}-2\cdot 20+80=48$$

$$F(40)=\frac{1}{50}\cdot 40^{2}-2\cdot 40+80=32$$

$$\frac{F\left(40\right)-F\left(20\right)}{40-20}=\frac{-16}{20}=-\frac{4}{5}$$

The average rate over that stretch is $-\frac{4}{5}$, not $-1$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The fuel use hits zero exactly when the quadratic has a real root, so the discriminant answers the question.

$$F(x)=\frac{1}{50}x^{2}-2x+80$$

$$\Delta=\left(-2\right)^{2}-4\left(\frac{1}{50}\right)\left(80\right)=-\frac{12}{5}$$

The extreme value of the model confirms the same picture.

$$F(50)=\frac{1}{50}\cdot 50^{2}-2\cdot 50+80=30$$

A negative discriminant keeps the whole graph on one side of the $x$-axis, out of reach of a zero fuel use, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The model turns any input into the fuel use, so a claim about one particular input is settled by a single substitution.

$$F(x)=\frac{1}{50}x^{2}-2x+80$$

$$F(100)=\frac{1}{50}\cdot 100^{2}-2\cdot 100+80=80$$

The model returns $80$ there, the figure named in the claim, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The story reduces to one formula and the quantities it links.

$$F(x)=\frac{1}{50}x^{2}-2x+80$$

The completed square hands over the turning point, and Vieta's relations hand over the sum and the product of the roots.

$$\text{vertex}=\left(50,30\right)\qquad S=100\qquad P=4000$$

A negative discriminant keeps the graph entirely on one side of the $x$-axis.

$$\Delta=-\frac{12}{5}$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $30$.

tasks.title: A Parabola Pinned by Its Vertex and One Point
tasks.context: A parabola $q$ has its vertex at $(3,-8)$ and passes through the point $(1,0)$; recover its rule before judging the claims. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The rule is $q(x)=2x^{2}-12x+10$.
The roots of $q$ are $1$ and $5$.
The graph of $q$ meets the $y$-axis at $y=10$.
The leading coefficient of $q$ is $2$.
The horizontal line $y=-8$ meets the graph of $q$ at two different points.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A vertex already fixes the shape up to one stretch factor, so write the parabola in completed-square form and let the extra point decide the factor.

$$q(x)=a\left(x-3\right)^{2}-8$$

Substituting the point $(1,0)$ leaves one equation for $a$.

$$0=a\left(1-3\right)^{2}-8\Rightarrow a=2$$

Expanding the square puts the rule in standard form.

$$q(x)=2x^{2}-12x+10$$

The rebuilt rule is the one printed in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The roots are the inputs where the graph touches the $x$-axis, so set the rule equal to zero; the discriminant says first how many such inputs exist.

$$q(x)=2x^{2}-12x+10$$

$$\Delta=\left(-12\right)^{2}-4\left(2\right)\left(10\right)=64$$

A positive discriminant gives two separate roots, delivered by the quadratic formula.

$$x_{1}=1\qquad x_{2}=5$$

The zeros are $1$ and $5$, the pair named in the claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The graph meets the $y$-axis where the input is zero, so the intercept is simply the constant term of the rule.

$$q(x)=2x^{2}-12x+10$$

$$q(0)=2\cdot 0^{2}-12\cdot 0+10=10$$

The graph cuts the $y$-axis at $y=10$, the height the claim names, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The leading coefficient is the number multiplying $x^{2}$ once every bracket has been multiplied out, and any minus sign in front belongs to it.

$$q(x)=2x^{2}-12x+10$$

$$a=2$$

Its sign tells the opening direction and its size tells how narrow the parabola is.

The leading coefficient is $2$, the number the claim gives, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

A horizontal line meets the parabola where the rule takes that constant value, so move the constant to the other side and count the solutions of the quadratic that is left.

$$q(x)+8=2x^{2}-12x+18$$

$$\Delta=\left(-12\right)^{2}-4\left(2\right)\left(18\right)=0$$

The turning point sits at height $-8$ and the arms open upwards, so the levels the graph reaches twice are exactly those above $-8$.

The level $y=-8$ is the height of the turning point itself, where the line touches the graph once instead of cutting it twice, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
A vertex already fixes the shape up to one stretch factor, so write the parabola in completed-square form and let the extra point decide the factor.

$$q(x)=a\left(x-3\right)^{2}-8$$

Substituting the point $(1,0)$ leaves one equation for $a$.

$$0=a\left(1-3\right)^{2}-8\Rightarrow a=2$$

Expanding the square puts the rule in standard form.

$$q(x)=2x^{2}-12x+10$$

Completing the square locates the turning point, and Vieta's relations give the sum $S$ and the product $P$ of the roots without solving anything.

$$\text{vertex}=\left(3,-8\right)\qquad S=6\qquad P=5$$

The discriminant comes out positive, so the graph cuts the $x$-axis twice, once on either side of the axis of symmetry.

$$\Delta=64\qquad x_{1}=1\qquad x_{2}=5$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-8$.

tasks.title: A Profit Curve With Two Break-Even Points
tasks.context: A workshop's monthly profit in hundreds of euros, when $x$ machines are produced, is modelled by $P(x)=-x^{2}+24x-80$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The profit is largest at $x=12$.
The largest possible profit equals $64$.
The profit is zero exactly at $x=4$ and $x=20$.
Between $x=0$ and $x=10$ the profit changes at an average rate of $14$ per unit of $x$.
At $x=2$ the profit equals $0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The profit follows a parabola, and a parabola turns exactly once: the best input is the abscissa of the turning point.

$$P(x)=-x^{2}+24x-80$$

$$x=-\frac{24}{2\cdot \left(-1\right)}=12$$

The leading coefficient $-1$ is negative, so the model rises to that input and falls afterwards.

The profit is therefore largest at $x=12$, the input in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The extreme profit is the height of the turning point, so find the input that produces it and evaluate the model there.

$$x=-\frac{24}{2\cdot \left(-1\right)}=12$$

$$P(12)=-12^{2}+24\cdot 12-80=64$$

Because the leading coefficient $-1$ is negative, this height is the largest value the model ever reaches.

The extreme profit is $64$, the figure the claim gives, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The profit vanishes where the model takes the value zero, so solve that quadratic equation.

$$P(x)=0$$

$$-x^{2}+24x-80=0$$

$$x_{1}=4\qquad x_{2}=20$$

The profit is zero exactly at those two inputs, as claimed, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

An average rate compares the change of the profit with the change of the input, so both endpoint values are needed first.

$$P(0)=-0^{2}+24\cdot 0-80=-80$$

$$P(10)=-10^{2}+24\cdot 10-80=60$$

$$\frac{P\left(10\right)-P\left(0\right)}{10-0}=\frac{140}{10}=14$$

The average rate over that stretch is $14$, the figure claimed, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The model turns any input into the profit, so a claim about one particular input is settled by a single substitution.

$$P(x)=-x^{2}+24x-80$$

$$P(2)=-2^{2}+24\cdot 2-80=-36$$

The model returns $-36$ there while the claim names $0$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The situation is captured by a single rule.

$$P(x)=-x^{2}+24x-80$$

Two standard readings cover most of what follows: the vertex from the completed square, and the sum and product of the roots from the coefficients.

$$\text{vertex}=\left(12,64\right)\qquad S=24\qquad P=80$$

Two real roots follow from the positive discriminant, and the axis of symmetry sits exactly halfway between them.

$$\Delta=256\qquad x_{1}=4\qquad x_{2}=20$$

The arms open downwards, so the turning point is the highest point of the graph and the largest value is $64$.

tasks.title: Half-Scaled Factors and the Values a Parabola Reaches
tasks.context: Consider $w(x)=\frac{1}{2}\left(x+1\right)\left(x-7\right)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The roots of $w$ are $-1$ and $7$.
The axis of symmetry of $w$ is the line $x=3$.
Expanding gives $w(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{2}-3x-\frac{7}{2}$.
The smallest value taken by $w$ is $-8$.
$w(x)\ge 0$ holds for every real $x$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The roots are the inputs where the graph touches the $x$-axis, so set the rule equal to zero; the discriminant says first how many such inputs exist.

$$w(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{2}-3x-\frac{7}{2}$$

$$\Delta=\left(-3\right)^{2}-4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{7}{2}\right)=16$$

A positive discriminant gives two separate roots, delivered by the quadratic formula.

$$x_{1}=-1\qquad x_{2}=7$$

The zeros are $-1$ and $7$, the pair named in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A parabola is its own mirror image in one vertical line, and the abscissa of that line is settled by the first two coefficients alone.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$w(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{2}-3x-\frac{7}{2}$$

$$x=-\frac{-3}{2\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}=3$$

The mirror line is $x=3$, exactly the line named in the claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Expanding means multiplying every bracket out and collecting equal powers of $x$; nothing else about the function changes.

$$w(x)=\frac{1}{2}\left(x+1\right)\left(x-7\right)$$

$$w(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{2}-3x-\frac{7}{2}$$

Every coefficient of the expansion can now be compared with the one the claim displays.

The two rules agree in all three coefficients, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

A parabola reaches its extreme value at the turning point and nowhere else, so locate the axis first and then read the height there.

$$w(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{2}-3x-\frac{7}{2}$$

$$x=-\frac{-3}{2\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}=3$$

$$w(3)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3^{2}-3\cdot 3-\frac{7}{2}=-8$$

The leading coefficient $\frac{1}{2}$ is positive, so the arms rise on both sides and $-8$ is the smallest value the function ever takes; there is no largest one.

That extreme value is $-8$, exactly as claimed, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

An inequality that has to hold for every real $x$ is a statement about the extreme value of the parabola, so the turning point decides it.

$$x=-\frac{-3}{2\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}=3$$

$$w(3)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3^{2}-3\cdot 3-\frac{7}{2}=-8$$

The leading coefficient $\frac{1}{2}$ is positive, so the values never drop below $-8$.

$$w(x)\ge -8$$

The value $-8$ is taken at the turning point, which breaks the claimed bound $0$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
There is one graph to study, and it is a parabola.

$$w(x)=\frac{1}{2}\left(x+1\right)\left(x-7\right)$$

Multiplying out puts the same rule in standard form, where every coefficient can be read off directly.

$$w(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{2}-3x-\frac{7}{2}$$

The axis formula fixes the turning point, while the sum $S$ and the product $P$ of the roots come out of the coefficients with no equation to solve.

$$\text{vertex}=\left(3,-8\right)\qquad S=6\qquad P=-7$$

Because the discriminant is positive the parabola meets the $x$-axis in two points, and factoring recovers them.

$$\Delta=16\qquad x_{1}=-1\qquad x_{2}=7$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-8$.

tasks.title: Heights of a Stone Recorded Every Second
tasks.context: A stone is launched upwards and its height above the ground is measured once per second. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The first differences of the $y$-values are constant.
The second differences of the $y$-values are constant and equal to $-10$.
The table is produced by the rule $y=-5x^{2}+30x$.
The $y$-values in the table are largest at $x=3$.
Continuing the pattern, the value at $x=5$ is $25$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

With equally spaced inputs the differences of neighbouring outputs do all the work: constant first differences are the fingerprint of a line.

$$y:\ 0,\ 25,\ 40,\ 45,\ 40$$

$$\text{first differences}:\ 25,\ 15,\ 5,\ -5$$

The steps come in different sizes, which is exactly what non-constant first differences mean, so the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Differencing twice is the standard test for a parabola: the second differences of a quadratic rule are constant, and they are zero for a line.

$$\text{first differences}:\ 25,\ 15,\ 5,\ -5$$

$$\text{second differences}:\ -10,\ -10,\ -10$$

They are all equal to $-10$, the value the claim names, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Testing a proposed rule against a table is a matter of substitution: the rule has to reproduce every row, and for a rule of degree at most two three rows already pin it down.

$$y=-5x^{2}+30x$$

Running the claimed rule over the first rows gives

$$0\mapsto 0,\quad 1\mapsto 25,\quad 2\mapsto 40$$

Every row comes out right, which identifies the claimed rule as the one behind the table, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

A claim about the rows of the table is settled inside the table itself: compare the listed outputs and see where the extreme one sits.

$$y:\ 0,\ 25,\ 40,\ 45,\ 40$$

$$\text{largest listed value}=45$$

That value appears at $x=3$.

The largest entry of the table does sit at $x=3$, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True
