Continuing a table means continuing its rule, so identify the rule from the differences first and only then step one row further.

$$y=-5x^{2}+30x$$

$$y(5)=-5\cdot 5^{2}+30\cdot 5=25$$

The next row would read $25$, exactly the value claimed, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The table is the whole stem, so read it as a list of pairs.

$$\left(0,0\right),\ \left(1,25\right),\ \left(2,40\right),\ \left(3,45\right),\ \left(4,40\right)$$

The inputs are equally spaced, which makes the differences of neighbouring outputs the fastest diagnostic tool available.

$$\text{first}:\ 25,\ 15,\ 5,\ -5\qquad \text{second}:\ -10,\ -10,\ -10$$

The first differences move while the second ones stand still, the signature of a parabola; the constant second difference is twice the leading coefficient times the squared spacing.

$$y=-5x^{2}+30x$$

tasks.title: Undoing a Line Around a Parabola
tasks.context: Let $f$ be a non-constant linear function with inverse $f^{-1}$, and let $g$ be a quadratic function. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The inverse $f^{-1}$ is again a non-constant linear function.
The composite $g\circ f^{-1}$ is a quadratic function.
The composite $f^{-1}\circ g$ is a quadratic function.
The composite $g\circ f^{-1}$ always has the same roots as $g$.
The composite $f^{-1}\circ g$ always has the same axis of symmetry as $g$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write $f(x)=mx+q$ with $m\neq 0$ and undo it by solving $y=mx+q$ for $x$.

$$y=mx+q\iff x=\frac{y-q}{m}$$

The division is legitimate precisely because the line is non-constant, and the result is again a first-degree formula.

$$f^{-1}(y)=\frac{1}{m}y-\frac{q}{m}$$

Its slope is $1/m$, which is a non-zero number, so the inverse is not a constant function.

Undoing a non-constant line gives another non-constant line, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Nesting the inverse line inside the parabola substitutes a first-degree expression for $x$, so expand the square and collect the terms.

$$g\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)=a\left(\frac{x-q}{m}\right)^{2}+b\left(\frac{x-q}{m}\right)+c$$

The square of a first-degree expression reaches $x^{2}$ and stops there, and the coefficient it produces is the leading one of the composite.

$$\text{coefficient of }x^{2}=\frac{a}{m^{2}}\neq 0$$

It is non-zero because $a\neq 0$ and $m\neq 0$, so nothing cancels the square term.

The composite is again a parabola, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

In this order the parabola is computed first and the inverse line is applied afterwards, which merely rescales and shifts the values.

$$f^{-1}\left(g(x)\right)=\frac{g(x)-q}{m}$$

$$f^{-1}\left(g(x)\right)=\frac{a}{m}x^{2}+\frac{b}{m}x+\frac{c-q}{m}$$

The leading coefficient $a/m$ is again non-zero, so the square term survives the rescaling.

The composite is a parabola in this order as well, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Here the inverse line acts on the argument, so a root of the composite is an abscissa whose image under $f^{-1}$ is a root of $g$; the roots get moved rather than kept.

$$g\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)=0\iff f^{-1}(x)\text{ is a root of }g$$

Take the simplest concrete pair and follow the bookkeeping.

$$g(x)=x^{2}\qquad f(x)=x+1\implies f^{-1}(x)=x-1$$

$$g\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)=\left(x-1\right)^{2}$$

The composite vanishes at $x=1$ while $g$ vanishes at $x=0$, so the two root sets are different.

Substituting inside the parabola shifts its roots, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

In this order the line acts after the parabola, and an operation performed on the values can only stretch or slide the graph vertically.

$$f^{-1}\left(g(x)\right)=\frac{a}{m}x^{2}+\frac{b}{m}x+\frac{c-q}{m}$$

Both the leading and the middle coefficient are divided by the same non-zero number $m$, so the quotient that produces the axis is unchanged.

$$-\frac{b/m}{2\left(a/m\right)}=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

The composite has exactly the same axis of symmetry as $g$, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Everything is stated for a general parabola, so the reasoning runs on the structure of $ax^{2}+bx+c$ instead of on numbers.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}\qquad f^{-1}(x)=\frac{x-q}{m}$$

The axis of symmetry sits at $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$, so it follows the first two coefficients and ignores the constant term entirely. Nesting two polynomials multiplies their highest powers instead of adding them, so a line inside a parabola still leaves a parabola. Undoing a line gives another line, so wrapping it around a parabola cannot change the highest power that appears.

tasks.title: Mirroring a Line and a Parabola
tasks.context: Let $f$ be a linear function and $g$ a quadratic function, and consider the mirrored pair $\tilde f(x)=f(-x)$ and $\tilde g(x)=g(-x)$. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graphs of $\tilde f$ and $\tilde g$ meet exactly as often as those of $f$ and $g$.
If the graphs of $f$ and $g$ are tangent, then so are those of $\tilde f$ and $\tilde g$.
Mirroring in this way can turn two meetings into three.
The parabola $\tilde g$ always opens in the same direction as $g$.
The parabola $\tilde g$ always has the same axis of symmetry as $g$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Mirroring replaces $x$ by $-x$ in both formulas at once, so the equation for the common abscissas is transported by the same substitution.

$$\tilde f(x)=\tilde g(x)\iff f(-x)=g(-x)$$

Hence $x$ is a meeting abscissa of the mirrored pair exactly when $-x$ is a meeting abscissa of the original pair, and the assignment $x\mapsto -x$ pairs the two sets of solutions off one against one.

$$x\text{ solves the new equation}\iff -x\text{ solves the old one}$$

Reflection can neither create nor destroy a meeting, so the counts agree, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Tangency is the algebraic statement that the difference has a repeated root, so mirror the difference and inspect its shape.

$$\tilde g(x)-\tilde f(x)=\left(g-f\right)(-x)$$

If the original graphs are tangent at abscissa $h$, the difference is a perfect square times its leading coefficient.

$$g(x)-f(x)=a\left(x-h\right)^{2}\implies \left(g-f\right)(-x)=a\left(x+h\right)^{2}$$

The mirrored difference is again a square with the same leading coefficient, now with its repeated root at $-h$.

The reflected graphs touch at the mirrored abscissa, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The number of meetings is governed by the difference, and mirroring keeps that difference quadratic with the very same leading coefficient.

$$\left(g-f\right)(-x)=ax^{2}-\left(b-m\right)x+\left(c-q\right)$$

A quadratic equation has at most two real solutions, so three meetings are out of reach; and the correspondence $x\mapsto -x$ shows the count was preserved exactly anyway.

$$a\neq 0\implies\text{at most two solutions}$$

Two meetings stay two meetings under a reflection, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The opening direction depends only on the coefficient of $x^{2}$, so mirror the formula and read that coefficient off.

$$\tilde g(x)=a\left(-x\right)^{2}+b\left(-x\right)+c$$

$$\tilde g(x)=ax^{2}-bx+c$$

Squaring kills the minus sign, so the leading coefficient is still $a$ and its sign has not moved.

The mirrored parabola opens the same way as the original, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Reflecting across the vertical coordinate axis carries the axis of symmetry along with the graph, so compute where it lands.

$$\tilde g(x)=ax^{2}-bx+c\implies\text{axis }x=\frac{b}{2a}$$

The original axis is $x=-b/(2a)$, so the two lines are opposites of each other and coincide only when $b=0$.

$$g(x)=\left(x-1\right)^{2}\implies\tilde g(x)=\left(x+1\right)^{2}$$

In this example the axis jumps from $x=1$ to $x=-1$, two different vertical lines.

The axis is mirrored too, so it generally moves, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
No coefficients are fixed, so the letters $a$, $b$ and $c$ have to be handled through the formulas that hold for every parabola.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}\qquad \Delta=b^{2}-4ac$$

The axis of symmetry sits at $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$, so it follows the first two coefficients and ignores the constant term entirely. The discriminant counts the real roots: two while it is positive, one when it vanishes and none once it turns negative. Replacing $x$ by $-x$ reflects a graph in the $y$-axis, and a parabola survives that swap exactly when its middle coefficient vanishes.

Both graphs are reflected at once, so the question is always which feature survives a reflection.

tasks.title: How Many Points Pin Down a Curve?
tasks.context: Let $P$, $Q$ and $R$ be pairwise distinct points of the plane, no two of which lie on the same vertical line. No coordinates are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Exactly one linear function has both $P$ and $Q$ on its graph.
There is always at least one quadratic function having $P$, $Q$ and $R$ on its graph.
If $P$, $Q$ and $R$ are not collinear, then exactly one quadratic function has all three on its graph.
Infinitely many quadratic functions have both $P$ and $Q$ on their graphs.
A quadratic function and a linear function can agree at all three points.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Two points with different abscissas determine a slope, and the slope together with one of the points determines the whole line.

$$m=\frac{y_{Q}-y_{P}}{x_{Q}-x_{P}}$$

The denominator is non-zero because $P$ and $Q$ do not lie on a common vertical line, so this quotient is a genuine number; the intercept then has no freedom left.

$$q=y_{P}-m\,x_{P}$$

Any line through both points must have this slope and this intercept, so no second one is possible.

Exactly one linear function passes through the two points, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Three points with distinct abscissas are always matched by exactly one formula of the shape $Ax^{2}+Bx+C$, but nothing guarantees that $A$ comes out non-zero.

$$Ax_{P}^{2}+Bx_{P}+C=y_{P},\quad\text{and likewise for }Q\text{ and }R$$

If the three points happen to be collinear, that unique solution is the line through them, with a vanishing square coefficient.

$$(0,0),\;(1,1),\;(2,2)\implies A=0,\;B=1,\;C=0$$

A quadratic function needs a non-zero coefficient of $x^{2}$, so in this configuration there is no quadratic function at all through the three points.

Collinear triples admit only a line, so the existence claim fails in general, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The three interpolation conditions form a system in the unknown coefficients, and distinct abscissas make it solvable in exactly one way.

$$Ax_{P}^{2}+Bx_{P}+C=y_{P},\;Ax_{Q}^{2}+Bx_{Q}+C=y_{Q},\;Ax_{R}^{2}+Bx_{R}+C=y_{R}$$

Subtracting the equations in pairs eliminates $C$ and then $B$, leaving one value for $A$, after which $B$ and $C$ follow in turn; every step divides only by differences of the abscissas, which are non-zero.

$$A=0\iff P,\,Q,\,R\text{ are collinear}$$

Since the points are assumed not to be collinear, the value obtained for $A$ is non-zero and the interpolating formula really is a quadratic one.

There is one such quadratic function and no more, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Passing through two points leaves one degree of freedom, and it can be displayed explicitly: start from the line through $P$ and $Q$ and add a term that vanishes at both abscissas.

$$g_{\lambda}(x)=\lambda\left(x-x_{P}\right)\left(x-x_{Q}\right)+mx+q$$

At $x=x_{P}$ and $x=x_{Q}$ the first summand is zero, so every member of this family contains both points, while the coefficient of $x^{2}$ is $\lambda$.

$$\lambda\neq 0\implies g_{\lambda}\text{ is a quadratic function}$$

Different non-zero values of $\lambda$ give different functions, and there are infinitely many of them.

Infinitely many parabolas pass through the same two points, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Agreement at a point means the difference of the two functions vanishes there, so study that difference.

$$g(x)-f(x)=ax^{2}+\left(b-m\right)x+\left(c-q\right),\quad a\neq 0$$

This is a quadratic expression, so it can vanish at two abscissas at most; three distinct abscissas are one too many.

$$x_{P},\,x_{Q},\,x_{R}\text{ distinct}\implies\text{three roots needed}$$

The abscissas are pairwise different because no two of the points share a vertical line, so the required third root cannot exist.

A parabola and a line can agree at two points but never at three, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The points stay unnamed, so the question is one of counting conditions against unknown coefficients.

$$f(x)=mx+q\qquad g(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c,\quad a\neq 0$$

Two points with different abscissas settle exactly one line, and three non-collinear ones settle exactly one parabola.

The points stay anonymous, so only counting arguments can decide the claims.

tasks.title: Where the Difference Reaches Its Extreme
tasks.context: Let $f$ be a linear function with slope $m$, let $g$ be a quadratic function whose leading coefficient $a$ is nonzero, and set $d=g-f$. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Unless $m$ vanishes, the axis of $d$ differs from the axis of $g$.
The axis of $d$ never depends on $m$.
The coefficient of $x^{2}$ in $d$ equals $a$.
The function $d$ has a smallest value exactly when $a$ is positive.
If the graphs of $f$ and $g$ are tangent, then the vertex of $d$ lies on the horizontal coordinate axis.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Subtracting the line leaves the square term alone but shifts the middle coefficient by the slope, and the axis is built from exactly those two numbers.

$$d(x)=ax^{2}+\left(b-m\right)x+\left(c-q\right)$$

$$\text{axis of }d:\;x=-\frac{b-m}{2a}\qquad \text{axis of }g:\;x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

Subtracting one from the other leaves a single term, whose vanishing is controlled by the slope alone.

$$-\frac{b-m}{2a}-\left(-\frac{b}{2a}\right)=\frac{m}{2a}$$

As long as $m\neq 0$ this gap is non-zero, so the two axes are different vertical lines, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The axis of the difference was just computed, and the slope of the line sits right inside the formula.

$$\text{axis of }d:\;x=-\frac{b}{2a}+\frac{m}{2a}$$

Changing $m$ therefore slides that vertical line, and a concrete pair makes the movement visible.

$$g(x)=x^{2},\;m=0\implies\text{axis }x=0\qquad m=2\implies\text{axis }x=1$$

Tilting the subtracted line moves the lowest point of the difference sideways.

The axis of $d$ does depend on the slope, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

A line contributes an $x$ term and a constant and nothing else, so the square term of the difference is inherited untouched.

$$d(x)=\left(ax^{2}+bx+c\right)-\left(mx+q\right)$$

$$d(x)=ax^{2}+\left(b-m\right)x+\left(c-q\right)$$

Whatever slope and intercept the line has, the number in front of $x^{2}$ is still the leading coefficient of $g$, and it is non-zero.

That coefficient equals $a$ exactly, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Whether a parabola has a smallest value is decided by the direction in which it opens, and the difference opens the same way as $g$.

$$d(x)=a\left(x-h\right)^{2}+k$$

With $a>0$ the square is multiplied by a positive number, so the values never sink below the vertex height $k$, which is actually attained at $x=h$.

$$a>0\implies d(x)\ge k\qquad a<0\implies d(x)\le k$$

With $a<0$ the picture is turned over: $k$ becomes the largest value and the arms fall without bound, so no smallest value exists.

A minimum exists precisely in the case $a>0$, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Tangency of the two graphs means the equation $g(x)=f(x)$ has a repeated solution, that is, the difference has a double root.

$$d(x)=g(x)-f(x)=a\left(x-h\right)^{2}$$

No constant is left over, so the vertex of $d$ sits at height zero.

$$d(h)=0\implies\text{vertex}=\left(h,0\right)$$

A point of height zero lies on the horizontal coordinate axis, and $h$ is the abscissa where the line touches the parabola.

The vertex of the difference lands exactly on that axis, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Since $a$, $b$ and $c$ are never given numbers, each claim has to survive for every admissible choice of them.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}\qquad \Delta=b^{2}-4ac$$

The axis of symmetry sits at $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$, so it follows the first two coefficients and ignores the constant term entirely. The discriminant counts the real roots: two while it is positive, one when it vanishes and none once it turns negative. Completed-square form puts the turning point at $(h,k)$, and the sign of $a$ decides whether $k$ is the smallest or the largest value taken.

The difference of the two functions is given its own name, so watch which of its coefficients still depend on the line.

tasks.title: Signs of the Roots from Sum and Product
tasks.context: Let $g(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$ with nonzero $a$ have two distinct real roots; write $S$ for their sum and $P$ for their product. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $P$ is negative, then the two roots have opposite signs.
If $P$ is positive and $S$ is negative, then both roots are negative.
If $P$ is negative and $a$ is positive, then $g$ takes a negative value at the origin.
If $P$ is positive, then both roots must be positive.
If $S$ vanishes, then the roots are opposites of each other and the axis is the vertical coordinate axis.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Vieta's relations turn the coefficients into the sum and the product of the roots, and the product alone already records their signs.

$$S=x_{1}+x_{2}=-\frac{b}{a}\qquad P=x_{1}x_{2}=\frac{c}{a}$$

A product of two real numbers is negative only when the factors have opposite signs, since equal signs give a positive product and a zero factor gives zero.

$$P<0\implies x_{1}x_{2}<0\implies\text{one root}<0<\text{the other}$$

Geometrically the parabola then crosses the horizontal axis once on each side of the origin.

A negative product forces roots of opposite signs, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The product fixes whether the signs agree, and the sum then decides which sign it is.

$$P>0\implies x_{1}\text{ and }x_{2}\text{ have the same sign}$$

Two positive numbers would add up to something positive, so a negative sum rules that case out and only the negative one survives.

$$S<0\implies x_{1}+x_{2}<0\implies\text{both roots}<0$$

For instance $g(x)=x^{2}+3x+2$ has $P=2>0$ and $S=-3<0$, with roots $-1$ and $-2$.

The two conditions together force both roots to be negative, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The value at the origin is the constant term, and Vieta's second relation expresses that term through the product of the roots.

$$P=\frac{c}{a}\implies c=aP$$

With $a>0$ and $P<0$ the product $aP$ is negative, so the constant term is negative.

$$g(0)=c=aP<0$$

This matches the picture: an upward-opening parabola with one root on each side of the origin must dip below the horizontal axis in between, and the origin lies in that stretch.

The function takes a negative value at the origin, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A positive product only says the two roots share a sign; it does not say which sign, so one counterexample is enough.

$$g(x)=x^{2}+3x+2=\left(x+1\right)\left(x+2\right)$$

$$x_{1}=-1\qquad x_{2}=-2\qquad P=2>0$$

The roots are distinct and real, the product is positive, yet both roots are negative.

Positivity of the product leaves the negative case wide open, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

A vanishing sum makes the two roots opposites, and the axis of symmetry is always the half-sum of the roots.

$$S=x_{1}+x_{2}=0\implies x_{2}=-x_{1}$$

$$\text{axis}:\;x=-\frac{b}{2a}=\frac{S}{2}=0$$

The line $x=0$ is the vertical coordinate axis, and the two roots sit symmetrically on either side of it at equal distance.

$$S=0\implies b=0\implies g(x)=ax^{2}+c$$

Both halves of the claim hold together, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Arithmetic is unavailable here: the coefficients stay symbolic, so the axis formula has to be argued with rather than evaluated.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}\qquad S=-\frac{b}{a}\qquad P=\frac{c}{a}$$

The axis of symmetry sits at $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$, so it follows the first two coefficients and ignores the constant term entirely. Vieta's relations turn the coefficients into the sum and the product of the roots without solving any equation. The discriminant counts the real roots: two while it is positive, one when it vanishes and none once it turns negative.

tasks.title: Sliding a Line Until It Touches
tasks.context: Let $g(x)=x^{2}-2x-5$ and let $f_c(x)=x+c$ be the family of lines of slope one, where $c$ runs through $\mathbb{R}$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: There is exactly one value of $c$ for which the line touches the parabola at a single point.
When the line passes through the origin, it meets the parabola twice.
For every real $c$ the line meets the parabola.
All the lines of the family have the same slope.
Whatever $c$ is, the graphs meet at no more than two points.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The family slides a line of fixed slope up and down, and touching means the equation $g(x)=f_c(x)$ has a repeated solution, so form the difference and watch its discriminant.

$$x^{2}-2x-5-\left(x+c\right)=x^{2}-3x-\left(5+c\right)=0$$

$$\Delta(c)=9+4\left(5+c\right)=29+4c$$

This is a first-degree expression in the parameter, so it vanishes for one single value.

$$29+4c=0\implies c=-\frac{29}{4}$$

Exactly one member of the family touches the parabola, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Passing through the origin fixes the parameter, since the intercept of $f_c$ is $c$ itself.

$$f_c(0)=c=0\implies f_{0}(x)=x$$

Now count the solutions of the difference at that parameter value.

$$\Delta(0)=29>0$$

$$x=\frac{3\pm\sqrt{29}}{2}$$

A positive discriminant makes the square root a genuine positive number, so the two abscissas are real and different.

The line through the origin cuts the parabola twice, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Whether a member meets the parabola is decided by the sign of the same discriminant, now read as a function of the shift.

$$\Delta(c)=29+4c$$

$$c<-\frac{29}{4}\implies \Delta(c)<0$$

Taking $c=-10$, for instance, gives a negative value.

$$\Delta(-10)=29-40=-11<0$$

With no real solution left the line has slid too far down and shares no point with the curve.

Sufficiently low members of the family miss the parabola entirely, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The parameter enters $f_c$ only as an added constant, so it never touches the coefficient of $x$.

$$f_c(x)=x+c$$

$$f_c\left(x_{2}\right)-f_c\left(x_{1}\right)=x_{2}-x_{1}$$

The rate of change is $1$ for every $c$, so all the members are parallel and the whole family is just one line sliding vertically.

Every line of the family has slope one, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The common abscissas are the real roots of the difference, so look at what kind of equation that difference gives.

$$g(x)-f_c(x)=x^{2}-3x-\left(5+c\right)$$

The parameter only shifts the constant term; the coefficient of $x^{2}$ stays $1$ for every $c$, so the equation remains quadratic.

$$\text{leading coefficient}=1\neq 0\implies\text{at most two real roots}$$

Depending on the sign of the discriminant the count is two, one or none, but it can never be three.

Two meetings is the maximum, whatever the shift, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: $g-f_c=x^{2}-3x-(5+c)$ with discriminant $29+4c$: two meetings, one, or none.

tasks.title: Choosing the Leading Coefficient
tasks.context: Let $g_a(x)=ax^{2}+2x-3$ with $a\neq 0$ and let $f(x)=x+1$. Consider what the real parameter $a$ can do. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: There is a value of $a$ for which the line is tangent to the parabola.
For every $a\neq 0$ the graphs meet at two distinct points.
Some choice of $a$ makes the graphs miss each other entirely.
The axis of symmetry of $g_a$ is the same for all admissible $a$.
Every parabola of the family crosses the $y$-axis at the same point.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Here the parameter is the leading coefficient itself, so form the difference and treat its discriminant as a function of $a$.

$$ax^{2}+2x-3-\left(x+1\right)=ax^{2}+x-4=0$$

$$\Delta(a)=1+16a$$

Tangency asks for a repeated root, that is a vanishing discriminant, which again is a first-degree condition on the parameter.

$$1+16a=0\implies a=-\frac{1}{16}$$

This value is real and non-zero, so it is an admissible member of the family.

One parabola of the family touches the line, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Two distinct meetings require a strictly positive discriminant, so check whether that holds for every admissible parameter.

$$\Delta(a)=1+16a$$

$$a<-\frac{1}{16}\implies \Delta(a)<0$$

Taking $a=-1$ gives a negative number, so that member has no real meeting abscissa at all.

$$\Delta(-1)=1-16=-15<0$$

Sufficiently negative leading coefficients destroy both intersections, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Missing each other is the case of a negative discriminant, and the discriminant moves along a straight line as the parameter varies.

$$\Delta(a)=1+16a<0\iff a<-\frac{1}{16}$$

Any parameter below that threshold works; with $a=-1$ the difference has no real root.

$$-x^{2}+x-4=0\implies \Delta=1-16=-15<0$$

The corresponding parabola opens downwards and stays entirely below the line.

Such a choice of the leading coefficient exists, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The axis of a parabola is computed from its first two coefficients, and here only the leading one carries the parameter.

$$x=-\frac{2}{2a}=-\frac{1}{a}$$

The result depends on $a$, so different members have different axes.

$$a=1\implies x=-1\qquad a=2\implies x=-\frac{1}{2}$$

The axis slides as the leading coefficient changes, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The crossing with the vertical coordinate axis is the value at $x=0$, and the parameter multiplies $x^{2}$, which vanishes there.

$$g_a(0)=a\cdot 0+2\cdot 0-3=-3$$

So every member of the family reaches the same height at $x=0$, however large or small the leading coefficient is.

$$a=1\implies g_{1}(0)=-3\qquad a=-5\implies g_{-5}(0)=-3$$

The whole family therefore pivots through the single point $(0,-3)$.

All of them cross the $y$-axis at that same point, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: $g_a-f=ax^{2}+x-4$ with discriminant $1+16a$; all curves pass through $(0,-3)$.

tasks.title: Coefficient Match Against a Composition
tasks.context: Let $f(x)=5x+1$ and $g(x)=3x^{2}-2x-1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Matching $g=Af^{2}+Bf+C$ forces $A=\frac{3}{25}$.
Matching $g=Af^{2}+Bf+C$ forces $B=-2$.
The highest power of $x$ in the nested function $f(g(x))$ is $x^{2}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write $g(x)=A f(x)^{2}+B f(x)+C$ and compare the two sides term by term. Only the first summand can create an $x^{2}$ term, and squaring the line contributes $5^{2}x^{2}$.

$$A\cdot 5^{2}=3$$

$$A=\frac{3}{25}$$

Equating the $x$ coefficients and then the constant terms gives the two remaining numbers.

$$B=-\frac{16}{25},\quad C=-\frac{12}{25}$$

These are the forced values the claim reports, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Write $g(x)=A f(x)^{2}+B f(x)+C$ and compare the two sides term by term. Only the first summand can create an $x^{2}$ term, and squaring the line contributes $5^{2}x^{2}$.

$$A\cdot 5^{2}=3$$

$$A=\frac{3}{25}$$

Equating the $x$ coefficients and then the constant terms gives the two remaining numbers.

$$B=-\frac{16}{25},\quad C=-\frac{12}{25}$$

The claim reports $B=-2$ instead of these forced values, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Applying the line to the parabola multiplies the parabola by the slope and then adds the intercept, so no new power of $x$ can be created.

$$f\left(g(x)\right)=5\left(3 x^{2} - 2 x - 1\right)+1$$

Expanding the bracket keeps the highest power exactly where it was.

$$f\left(g(x)\right)=15 x^{2} - 10 x - 4$$

The highest power is $x^{2}$ with coefficient $15\neq 0$, so the nested function is again a parabola, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

A nested value is computed from the inside outwards: evaluate the inner function at the given number first, then feed the result into the outer function.

$$f(0)=5\cdot 0+1=1$$

That output now becomes the input of $g$.

$$g(1)=3\cdot 1^{2}-2\cdot 1-1=0$$

The nested value is $0$, the number claimed, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Nesting is not symmetric: feeding the line into the parabola need not agree with feeding the parabola into the line, so each order has to be computed on its own, working from the inside outwards.

$$g(0)=-1\qquad f\left(-1\right)=-4$$

$$f(0)=1\qquad g\left(1\right)=0$$

The two orders give $-4$ and $0$, which are different numbers, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Both rules are handed over with numbers already in place:

$$f(x)=5 x + 1\qquad g(x)=3 x^{2} - 2 x - 1$$

Rewriting $g$ as $a(x-h)^{2}+k$ exposes the vertex, with $h$ taken from the axis formula and $k$ obtained by substituting that abscissa back in.

$$g(x)=3\left(x-\frac{1}{3}\right)^{2}-\frac{4}{3}\qquad \text{vertex}=\left(\frac{1}{3},-\frac{4}{3}\right)$$

Because $f$ is a line with non-zero slope, the square $f(x)^{2}$ already carries an $x^{2}$ term, so $g$ can be rebuilt from $f(x)^{2}$, $f(x)$ and a constant. Matching coefficients gives

$$A=\frac{3}{25},\quad B=-\frac{16}{25},\quad C=-\frac{12}{25}$$

tasks.title: Root Spacing Against the Axis of a Parabola
tasks.context: The parabola $p$ is given by $p(x)=x^{2}+3x-40$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The distance between the two roots of $p$ is $13$.
The axis of symmetry of $p$ is the line $x=-\frac{3}{2}$.
The two roots of $p$ add up to $3$.
The two roots of $p$ multiply to $-40$.
$p$ is increasing for every $x>-2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The two roots sit symmetrically on either side of the axis, so their gap is the square root of the discriminant divided by the size of the leading coefficient.

$$\left|x_{1}-x_{2}\right|=\frac{\sqrt{\Delta}}{\left|a\right|}$$

$$\Delta=3^{2}-4\left(1\right)\left(-40\right)=169$$

$$\left|x_{1}-x_{2}\right|=\frac{13}{1}=13$$

The roots $-8$ and $5$ are indeed $13$ apart.

The gap is $13$, the distance the claim reports, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A parabola is its own mirror image in one vertical line, and the abscissa of that line is settled by the first two coefficients alone.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}+3x-40$$

$$x=-\frac{3}{2\cdot 1}=-\frac{3}{2}$$

The mirror line is $x=-\frac{3}{2}$, exactly the line named in the claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Vieta's relations read the sum of the two roots straight off the coefficients, with no equation to solve: it is minus the middle coefficient divided by the leading one.

$$S=-\frac{b}{a}$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}+3x-40$$

$$S=-\frac{3}{1}=-3$$

The roots themselves are $-8$ and $5$, and they do add up to $-3$.

The sum is $-3$ while the claim reports $3$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The second of Vieta's relations gives the product of the roots as the constant term divided by the leading coefficient.

$$P=\frac{c}{a}$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}+3x-40$$

$$P=\frac{-40}{1}=-40$$

Multiplying the roots $-8$ and $5$ confirms the value.

The product is $-40$, exactly what the claim reports, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

A parabola changes direction exactly once, at its axis, so a claim about a whole half-line is decided by where that axis sits.

$$p(x)=x^{2}+3x-40$$

$$x=-\frac{3}{2\cdot 1}=-\frac{3}{2}$$

With a positive leading coefficient the graph falls on everything to the left of $x=-\frac{3}{2}$ and rises on everything to its right.

The half-line $x>-2$ reaches across the axis $x=-\frac{3}{2}$, where the direction changes, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
There is one graph to study, and it is a parabola.

$$p(x)=x^{2}+3x-40$$

The axis formula fixes the turning point, while the sum $S$ and the product $P$ of the roots come out of the coefficients with no equation to solve.

$$\text{vertex}=\left(-\frac{3}{2},-\frac{169}{4}\right)\qquad S=-3\qquad P=-40$$

The discriminant comes out positive, so the graph cuts the $x$-axis twice, once on either side of the axis of symmetry.

$$\Delta=169\qquad x_{1}=-8\qquad x_{2}=5$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-\frac{169}{4}$.

tasks.title: A Translation Cannot Flatten a Parabola
tasks.context: Let $f(x)=-6x+4$ and $g(x)=2x^{2}+3x-2$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Completing the square gives $g(x)=2\left(x+\frac{3}{4}\right)^{2}-\frac{25}{8}$.
Some vertical translation of $g$ makes $f-g$ a constant function.
The vertex of the graph of $g$ is $\left(-\frac{3}{4},-\frac{25}{8}\right)$.
The average rate of change of $g$ on $[0,2]$ equals the slope of $y=f(x)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Completing the square rewrites a parabola as $a(x-h)^{2}+k$, where $h$ is the abscissa of the axis of symmetry and $k$ is the height of the vertex, so both numbers have to be produced first.

$$g(x)=2 x^{2} + 3 x - 2$$

The axis comes from the first two coefficients.

$$x=-\frac{3}{2\cdot 2}=-\frac{3}{4}$$

The vertex height is the value of $g$ on that axis.

$$g\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)=2\cdot \left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)^{2}+3\cdot \left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)-2=-\frac{25}{8}$$

Putting the leading coefficient, the shift and the height together gives

$$g(x)=2\left(x+\frac{3}{4}\right)^{2}-\frac{25}{8}$$

This is the very expression the claim displays, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Translating a graph vertically adds a fixed number to its formula, which changes the constant term and nothing else, so the $x^{2}$ term of the difference survives untouched.

$$f(x)-g(x)=- 2 x^{2} - 9 x + 6$$

Shifting $g$ by any real $t$ replaces $g$ by $g+t$ in that difference.

$$f(x)-\left(g(x)+t\right)=- 2 x^{2} - 9 x + 6-t$$

The coefficient of $x^{2}$ stays $-2$ for every shift $t$, so the difference remains a genuine parabola and never flattens out, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The vertex of a parabola lies on its axis of symmetry, whose abscissa is read from the first two coefficients, and its height is the value of the function there.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$g(x)=2 x^{2} + 3 x - 2$$

$$x=-\frac{3}{2\cdot 2}=-\frac{3}{4}$$

Evaluating $g$ on the axis gives the height.

$$g\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)=2\cdot \left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)^{2}+3\cdot \left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)-2=-\frac{25}{8}$$

Because the leading coefficient $2$ is positive, the arms rise on both sides and this point is the lowest on the graph.

The vertex is $\left(-\frac{3}{4},-\frac{25}{8}\right)$, precisely the point named in the claim, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The average rate of change over an interval is the slope of the chord joining the two endpoint values, so evaluate $g$ at both ends and divide by the width of the interval.

$$\frac{g(2)-g(0)}{2-0}$$

$$g(0)=-2\qquad g(2)=12$$

$$\frac{12-\left(-2\right)}{2}=7$$

The line is compared through its own slope, the coefficient of $x$.

$$f(x)=4 - 6 x$$

The chord slope is $7$ while the line has slope $-6$, two different numbers, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

A nested value is computed from the inside outwards: evaluate the inner function at the given number first, then feed the result into the outer function.

$$g(0)=2\cdot 0^{2}+3\cdot 0-2=-2$$

That output now becomes the input of $f$.

$$f\left(-2\right)=-6\cdot \left(-2\right)+4=16$$

The nested value is $16$, the number claimed, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Everything starts from the two concrete rules

$$f(x)=4 - 6 x\qquad g(x)=2 x^{2} + 3 x - 2$$

The slope, the vertical intercepts and the opening direction all sit in plain view in the coefficients; the arms go upwards.

$$m=-6\qquad f(0)=4\qquad g(0)=-2\qquad a=2$$

Completing the square moves the turning point of the parabola into view: the axis comes from the first two coefficients and the height is the value of $g$ there.

$$g(x)=2\left(x+\frac{3}{4}\right)^{2}-\frac{25}{8}\qquad \text{vertex}=\left(-\frac{3}{4},-\frac{25}{8}\right)$$

Comparing the two graphs means solving $f(x)=g(x)$, a quadratic equation whose discriminant reports two real solutions.

$$f(x)-g(x)=- 2 x^{2} - 9 x + 6\qquad \Delta=129$$

tasks.title: Lines Through the Vertex
tasks.context: Let $g$ be a quadratic function with vertex $V$ and nonzero leading coefficient $a$, and let $f$ be a linear function with slope $m$ whose graph passes through $V$. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $m$ vanishes, then $V$ is the only common point of the two graphs.
If $m$ is nonzero, then the graphs have a second common point different from $V$.
Whatever $m$ is, the two graphs are tangent at $V$.
The two graphs always have at least one common point.
When a second common point exists, it lies to the right of the axis of $g$ exactly when $m$ and $a$ have the same sign.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Put the parabola in vertex form around $V=(h,k)$; a line of slope zero through $V$ is simply the horizontal line at that height.

$$g(x)=a\left(x-h\right)^{2}+k\qquad f(x)=k$$

The difference is then a pure square, so the meeting condition has a repeated solution and no other.

$$g(x)-f(x)=a\left(x-h\right)^{2}=0\iff x=h$$

Away from $x=h$ the square is strictly positive and $a\neq 0$, so the difference never returns to zero.

The vertex is the one and only common point in that case, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A line through the vertex can be written using the same shifted variable, and then the difference factors by hand.

$$f(x)=m\left(x-h\right)+k$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=a\left(x-h\right)^{2}-m\left(x-h\right)=\left(x-h\right)\left(a\left(x-h\right)-m\right)$$

The first factor gives back the vertex; the second one vanishes at an abscissa obtained by dividing the slope by the leading coefficient.

$$a\left(x-h\right)=m\iff x=h+\frac{m}{a}$$

Because $m\neq 0$ and $a\neq 0$ the shift $m/a$ is non-zero, so this second abscissa really is different from $h$.

A second common point appears as soon as the line is tilted, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Tangency would mean the factored difference has a repeated root at the vertex, so look at the factorisation once more.

$$g(x)-f(x)=\left(x-h\right)\left(a\left(x-h\right)-m\right)$$

For $m\neq 0$ the factor $x-h$ occurs only once, so the difference changes sign at $x=h$ and the graphs cross there instead of touching.

$$g(x)=x^{2},\;f(x)=x\implies g(x)-f(x)=x\left(x-1\right)$$

In this example the line through the vertex $(0,0)$ cuts the parabola again at $x=1$, and near the origin the difference is negative on one side and positive on the other.

Only the horizontal choice $m=0$ produces a genuine tangency, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The line is required to pass through the vertex, so one common point is handed over by the hypothesis itself.

$$f(h)=k=g(h)$$

Both graphs therefore contain the point $V=(h,k)$, whatever the slope $m$ and the leading coefficient $a$ happen to be.

$$g(x)-f(x)=\left(x-h\right)\left(a\left(x-h\right)-m\right)$$

Algebraically the factor $x-h$ is always present in the difference, so the meeting can never be lost.

At least the vertex is always shared, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The second meeting was located exactly, so its position relative to the axis $x=h$ is a matter of one sign.

$$x_{2}=h+\frac{m}{a}$$

The point lies to the right of the axis precisely when the added shift is positive, and a quotient of two non-zero numbers is positive exactly when they share a sign.

$$x_{2}>h\iff\frac{m}{a}>0\iff m\text{ and }a\text{ have the same sign}$$

Opposite signs push the second meeting to the left instead, at the mirrored distance from the axis.

The criterion is exactly the agreement of the two signs, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Everything is stated for a general parabola, so the reasoning runs on the structure of $ax^{2}+bx+c$ instead of on numbers.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}\qquad \Delta=b^{2}-4ac$$

The axis of symmetry sits at $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$, so it follows the first two coefficients and ignores the constant term entirely. The discriminant counts the real roots: two while it is positive, one when it vanishes and none once it turns negative. Completed-square form puts the turning point at $(h,k)$, and the sign of $a$ decides whether $k$ is the smallest or the largest value taken.

The line is pinned to the vertex $V$, so one common point is there before any computation starts.

tasks.title: Composing a Parabola With Itself
tasks.context: Let $f$ be a non-constant linear function and let $g$ be a quadratic function. Consider the compositions $g\circ g$ and $g\circ f\circ g$. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The highest power of $x$ in $g\circ g$ is $x^{4}$.
The highest power of $x$ in $g\circ f\circ g$ is $x^{4}$.
The highest power of $x$ in $g\circ g$ is $x^{4}$ because the two powers are added rather than multiplied.
The composition $f\circ f$ is again a non-constant linear function.
For a suitable $g$, the composition $g\circ g$ is a quadratic function.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Nesting substitutes the whole parabola in place of $x$, so the square term gets squared and that is where the top power comes from.

$$g\left(g(x)\right)=a\left(ax^{2}+bx+c\right)^{2}+b\left(ax^{2}+bx+c\right)+c$$

Squaring an expression whose highest power is $x^{2}$ reaches $x^{4}$, with a coefficient that is a product of non-zero numbers.

$$a\left(ax^{2}\right)^{2}=a^{3}x^{4}$$

The remaining summands only climb to $x^{2}$, so nothing can cancel the $a^{3}x^{4}$ term.

The highest power really is $x^{4}$, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Work from the inside out: applying the line to the parabola only rescales it, and then the outer parabola squares the result.

$$f\left(g(x)\right)=m\left(ax^{2}+bx+c\right)+q$$

The leading coefficient here is $ma$, non-zero because the line is non-constant, so the middle stage is still a parabola.

$$g\left(f\left(g(x)\right)\right)=a\left(ma\,x^{2}+\dots\right)^{2}+\dots$$

$$\text{coefficient of }x^{4}=a\left(ma\right)^{2}=a^{3}m^{2}\neq 0$$

The triple nesting also tops out at $x^{4}$, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The value $x^{4}$ is right, but the reason offered is not: powers of nested functions multiply, and here $2$ times $2$ happens to agree with $2$ plus $2$.

$$2\cdot 2=4\qquad 2+2=4$$

A single case where the two rules disagree exposes which one is at work: nest the parabola inside the line and count.

$$g\left(f(x)\right)=a\left(mx+q\right)^{2}+b\left(mx+q\right)+c$$

$$\text{highest power}=x^{2}:\quad 2\cdot 1=2\text{, not }2+1=3$$

Adding the powers is the rule for multiplying two formulas together, not for nesting one inside the other.

The stated justification is the wrong rule, even though the number it produces here is right, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Nesting a line inside itself substitutes a first-degree expression into a first-degree formula, so expand and collect.

$$f\left(f(x)\right)=m\left(mx+q\right)+q$$

$$f\left(f(x)\right)=m^{2}x+q\left(m+1\right)$$

The new slope is $m^{2}$, and a square of a non-zero number is non-zero, so the result is a line that is not constant.

$$m\neq 0\implies m^{2}>0$$

The double nesting stays a non-constant line, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

For the nesting to collapse to a parabola, the $x^{4}$ term would have to disappear, so look at the coefficient it carries.

$$g\left(g(x)\right)=a\left(ax^{2}+bx+c\right)^{2}+b\left(ax^{2}+bx+c\right)+c$$

$$\text{coefficient of }x^{4}=a^{3}$$

This vanishes only when $a=0$, which is forbidden because $g$ is a parabola; no choice of $b$ or $c$ has any influence on it.

$$a\neq 0\implies a^{3}\neq 0$$

The $x^{4}$ term is always there, so the nesting is never a parabola, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
No numbers appear, so the claims are settled by what nesting does to the highest power of $x$.

$$f(x)=mx+q\qquad g(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c,\quad a\neq 0$$

Nesting multiplies the highest powers instead of adding them, so feeding a parabola into a parabola reaches $x^{4}$, and inserting a line between them changes nothing about that.

Here a parabola is nested inside a parabola, not merely a line inside one.

tasks.title: Can a Line Trap a Parabola?
tasks.context: Let $g$ be a quadratic function whose leading coefficient $a$ is nonzero, and let $f$ be a linear function. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $a$ is positive, some line lies strictly below the whole graph of $g$.
If $a$ is positive, some line lies strictly above the whole graph of $g$.
If $a$ is positive, then $g-f$ attains a smallest value for every linear $f$.
If $a$ is negative, some horizontal line lies strictly above the whole graph of $g$.
The graph of $g$ can be squeezed between two distinct parallel lines over all of $\mathbb{R}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

An upward-opening parabola has a lowest point, and any level below that height gives a line the graph never reaches.

$$g(x)=a\left(x-h\right)^{2}+k\ge k\quad\text{for all }x,\qquad a>0$$

Take the horizontal line one unit under the vertex; it is a perfectly legitimate linear function.

$$f(x)=k-1\implies g(x)-f(x)\ge 1>0$$

The gap between the two graphs is at least one unit everywhere, so the line stays strictly below the parabola.

Such a line exists, for instance that horizontal one, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

A line above the whole graph would need $g(x)<f(x)$ for every $x$, so examine the difference far from the origin.

$$g(x)-f(x)=ax^{2}+\left(b-m\right)x+\left(c-q\right),\quad a>0$$

The difference is itself an upward-opening parabola, so it has a lowest point and then climbs beyond every bound on both sides.

$$g(x)-f(x)>0\text{ for all }|x|\text{ large enough}$$

The arms of the parabola therefore rise past any line eventually, no matter how steep the line is chosen.

No line can stay above the whole graph when $a>0$, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Subtracting a line changes only the $x$ term and the constant term, so the difference keeps the leading coefficient of $g$.

$$g(x)-f(x)=ax^{2}+\left(b-m\right)x+\left(c-q\right),\quad a>0$$

Completing the square exhibits a non-negative square multiplied by a positive number, plus a constant that is actually attained at the vertex.

$$g(x)-f(x)=a\left(x-h_{d}\right)^{2}+k_{d}\ge k_{d}$$

The value $k_{d}$ depends on the line chosen, but for each line it is a genuine number reached at one abscissa.

The difference attains a smallest value for every linear $f$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

A negative leading coefficient turns the arms downwards, so the vertex is now the highest point of the graph.

$$g(x)=a\left(x-h\right)^{2}+k\le k\quad\text{for all }x,\qquad a<0$$

The square is non-negative and $a<0$, so the product is at most zero and the values never climb past the vertex height $k$.

$$f(x)=k+1\implies f(x)-g(x)\ge 1>0$$

The horizontal line one unit above the vertex therefore misses the graph entirely and stays above it.

Such a horizontal line exists, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

A strip between two parallel lines has bounded width, so being squeezed inside it would keep the difference to one of those lines bounded.

$$f_{1}(x)=mx+q_{1}\qquad f_{2}(x)=mx+q_{2}$$

Subtracting the lower line from $g$ leaves a parabola with the same leading coefficient $a\neq 0$, and such a difference is unbounded.

$$g(x)-f_{1}(x)=ax^{2}+\left(b-m\right)x+\left(c-q_{1}\right)$$

For $a>0$ its values exceed $q_{2}-q_{1}$ once $|x|$ is large, and for $a<0$ they fall below the strip instead, so the graph escapes on one side or the other.

A parabola always breaks out of a strip of finite width, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The parabola arrives already centred on its vertex, so the reasoning stays with the roles of $a$, $h$ and $k$.

$$g(x)=a\left(x-h\right)^{2}+k$$

Completed-square form puts the turning point at $(h,k)$, and the sign of $a$ decides whether $k$ is the smallest or the largest value taken. Far out on either side the $x^{2}$ term outgrows every linear term, so the parabola decides who ends up on top.

tasks.title: Reading Roots Through a Linear Substitution
tasks.context: Let $f$ be a non-constant linear function with slope $m$, let $q(y)=Ay^{2}+By+C$ with nonzero $A$, and set $g=q\circ f$. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The function $g$ is a quadratic function.
Every real root of $g$ is a point at which $f$ takes a root value of $q$.
If $q$ has no real roots, then $g$ has no real roots.
The roots of $g$ coincide with the roots of $q$.
The coefficient of $x^{2}$ in $g$ equals $A$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Substituting the line into the outer formula replaces $y$ by a first-degree expression, so expand and collect the powers of $x$.

$$g(x)=A\left(mx+k\right)^{2}+B\left(mx+k\right)+C$$

$$g(x)=Am^{2}x^{2}+\left(2Amk+Bm\right)x+\left(Ak^{2}+Bk+C\right)$$

The coefficient of $x^{2}$ is the product $Am^{2}$, and both factors are non-zero: $A$ by hypothesis and $m$ because the line is non-constant.

The substitution produces a genuine quadratic function, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The composite is evaluated in two stages, so a zero of the whole thing is a zero produced at the second stage.

$$g\left(x_{0}\right)=q\left(f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$$

If this number is zero then the value $y_{0}=f(x_{0})$ satisfies $q(y_{0})=0$, so it is one of the roots of $q$.

$$g\left(x_{0}\right)=0\iff q\left(y_{0}\right)=0,\quad y_{0}=f\left(x_{0}\right)$$

The reasoning uses nothing but the definition of nesting, so it applies to every real root of $g$.

Each root of the composite is an abscissa where the line hits a root of $q$, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The composite can only reach values that $q$ itself takes, so a $q$ that never vanishes hands its property straight over.

$$q(y)\neq 0\text{ for every real }y$$

For any real $x$ the number $f(x)$ is real, so $q$ evaluated there is non-zero as well.

$$g(x)=q\left(f(x)\right)\neq 0\quad\text{for all real }x$$

In terms of discriminants, $q$ having none means its graph misses the horizontal axis, and substituting a line cannot pull it back down.

The composite has no real roots either, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The roots of the composite are the abscissas whose image under $f$ is a root of $q$, so they are the roots of $q$ pulled back through the line.

$$g(x)=0\iff f(x)\text{ is a root of }q\iff x=f^{-1}\left(\text{root}\right)$$

One concrete pair shows the shift at once.

$$f(x)=x+1\qquad q(y)=y^{2}\implies g(x)=\left(x+1\right)^{2}$$

The only root of $q$ is $0$, while the only root of $g$ is $-1$, so the two sets do not coincide.

The line moves the roots unless it happens to be the identity, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The expansion already displays the leading coefficient of the composite, and the slope of the line is squared into it.

$$g(x)=Am^{2}x^{2}+\left(2Amk+Bm\right)x+\left(Ak^{2}+Bk+C\right)$$

So the coefficient of $x^{2}$ is $Am^{2}$, which equals $A$ only in the special case $m^{2}=1$.

$$m=2\implies\text{coefficient of }x^{2}=4A\neq A\text{ unless }A=0$$

Since $A\neq 0$ is assumed, a slope such as $m=2$ genuinely changes the number in front of $x^{2}$.

The leading coefficient is $Am^{2}$, not $A$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Nothing is numeric here, so the sign of the discriminant is the only lever available.

$$\Delta=b^{2}-4ac$$

The discriminant counts the real roots: two while it is positive, one when it vanishes and none once it turns negative. Nesting two polynomials multiplies their highest powers instead of adding them, so a line inside a parabola still leaves a parabola.

The parabola arrives as a second function wrapped around a line, so the substitution has to be unwound before the roots can be read.

tasks.title: Equal Values and the Axis
tasks.context: Let $g$ be a quadratic function with nonzero leading coefficient and axis of symmetry $\ell$, and let $u$ and $v$ be distinct real numbers with $g(u)=g(v)$. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The line $\ell$ passes through the midpoint of $u$ and $v$.
The numbers $u$ and $v$ must be the roots of $g$.
For every positive real $t$, the two points at distance $t$ from $\ell$ on either side carry equal values of $g$.
The sum $u+v$ is determined by the coefficients of $g$ alone.
Such a pair of distinct numbers with equal values exists for every quadratic $g$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Two equal values give an equation between the coefficients, so subtract the two evaluations and factor.

$$g(u)-g(v)=a\left(u^{2}-v^{2}\right)+b\left(u-v\right)$$

$$g(u)-g(v)=\left(u-v\right)\left(a\left(u+v\right)+b\right)$$

The first factor is non-zero because $u$ and $v$ are distinct, so the second one must vanish, which pins down the sum.

$$a\left(u+v\right)+b=0\implies\frac{u+v}{2}=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

The right-hand side is exactly the abscissa of the axis of symmetry.

The axis passes through the midpoint of the two abscissas, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Equal values need not be zero values, so nothing forces the common value onto the horizontal axis.

$$g(x)=x^{2}\qquad u=1\qquad v=-1$$

$$g(1)=1=g(-1)$$

The hypothesis is satisfied with a common value of $1$, yet the only root of this parabola is $0$, which is neither $u$ nor $v$.

$$g(x)=0\iff x=0$$

Symmetric pairs of abscissas exist at every height, not only at height zero, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Vertex form makes the symmetry visible: only the distance from the axis enters, through a square.

$$g(x)=a\left(x-h\right)^{2}+k,\qquad\ell:\;x=h$$

Evaluating at the two abscissas $h+t$ and $h-t$ squares the same number up to sign, so the two results agree.

$$g\left(h+t\right)=at^{2}+k\qquad g\left(h-t\right)=at^{2}+k$$

This holds for every positive $t$, and the two abscissas are genuinely different because $t\neq 0$.

Points mirrored in the axis always carry the same value, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The relation derived from $g(u)=g(v)$ involved no data beyond the coefficients, so read it again.

$$\left(u-v\right)\left(a\left(u+v\right)+b\right)=0,\quad u\neq v$$

$$u+v=-\frac{b}{a}$$

Whatever pair of distinct abscissas with equal values one starts from, its sum is this one number, which is twice the abscissa of the axis.

The sum is fixed by $a$ and $b$ alone, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The axis of symmetry always exists, and it supplies such a pair for free.

$$h=-\frac{b}{2a}\qquad u=h+1\qquad v=h-1$$

These two numbers are distinct, and vertex form shows they carry the same value.

$$g\left(h+1\right)=a+k=g\left(h-1\right)$$

The construction only needs $a\neq 0$, which is part of being a quadratic function, so it works for every $g$ of this kind.

Such a pair can always be produced, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Arithmetic is unavailable here: the coefficients stay symbolic, so the axis formula has to be argued with rather than evaluated.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

The axis of symmetry sits at $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$, so it follows the first two coefficients and ignores the constant term entirely.

The axis carries its own name here, and every letter compares it with some other line.

tasks.title: A Pencil of Lines and Two Tangents
tasks.context: Let $g(x)=x^{2}-4x+6$ and let $f_t(x)=t(x-1)+2$ be the family of lines obtained as the real parameter $t$ varies. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Every line of the family passes through one and the same point.
There are exactly two slopes for which the line touches the parabola at a single point.
There are slopes for which the line misses the parabola completely.
For every slope the line meets the parabola at two distinct points.
The fixed point common to all the lines lies on the parabola.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The parameter multiplies the bracket $x-1$, so it loses all its influence wherever that bracket vanishes.

$$f_t(1)=t\cdot 0+2=2$$

Every member of the family therefore reaches the height $2$ at the abscissa $1$, whatever the slope.

$$t=0\implies f_{0}(x)=2\qquad t=3\implies f_{3}(x)=3x-1$$

Both of these pass through $(1,2)$, and the same computation works for any slope: the family is a pencil of lines hinged at that point.

One fixed point is common to all the lines, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Touching at a single point means the equation $g(x)=f_t(x)$ has a repeated solution, so collect the terms and set the discriminant to zero.

$$x^{2}-4x+6-t\left(x-1\right)-2=x^{2}-\left(4+t\right)x+\left(4+t\right)=0$$

$$\Delta(t)=\left(4+t\right)^{2}-4\left(4+t\right)=t\left(4+t\right)$$

The condition is now a quadratic equation in the slope, and it factors immediately.

$$t\left(4+t\right)=0\implies t=0\text{ or }t=-4$$

The first gives the horizontal line $y=2$ touching at the vertex $(2,2)$, the second the line $y=-4x+6$ touching at $(0,6)$.

There are exactly two such slopes, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

A member misses the parabola exactly when the discriminant is negative, so study the sign of the product just obtained.

$$\Delta(t)=t\left(4+t\right)$$

A product of two factors is negative when they have opposite signs, which happens strictly between the two roots.

$$-4<t<0\implies \Delta(t)<0$$

$$t=-2\implies \Delta(-2)=\left(-2\right)\cdot 2=-4<0$$

The line $y=-2x+4$ therefore shares no point with the curve.

Slopes in that window make the line miss the parabola, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Two distinct meetings need a strictly positive discriminant, and the discriminant has already been factored.

$$\Delta(t)=t\left(4+t\right)$$

It vanishes at $t=0$ and $t=-4$, where the line only touches the curve, and it is negative in between, where nothing is shared.

$$t=-2\implies \Delta=-4<0\qquad t=0\implies \Delta=0$$

Some slopes give one meeting and some give none, so two distinct meetings do not always occur, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The fixed point of the pencil was found to be $(1,2)$, so test whether the parabola reaches that height there.

$$g(1)=1-4+6=3$$

The parabola is at height $3$ while the fixed point sits at height $2$, so the point lies strictly below the curve.

$$\text{vertex of }g=\left(2,2\right)\quad\text{and}\quad g(1)=3\neq 2$$

That position is exactly what makes the two tangent lines and the window of missing lines possible.

The hinge point of the family is not on the parabola, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: $g-f_t=x^{2}-(4+t)x+(4+t)$ with discriminant $t(4+t)$: two tangent slopes, and no meeting in between.

tasks.title: Sliding the Parabola Sideways
tasks.context: Let $f(x)=2x-1$ and let $g_r(x)=(x-r)^{2}-4$ be the family of parabolas obtained as the real shift $r$ varies. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: There is exactly one shift for which the line is tangent to the parabola.
For sufficiently negative shifts the line and the parabola do not meet.
The vertex height of $g_r$ depends on $r$.
The axis of symmetry of $g_r$ moves as $r$ changes.
Every parabola of the family crosses the $y$-axis at the same point.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The family moves a fixed parabola left and right, and tangency means the equation $g_r(x)=f(x)$ has a repeated solution.

$$\left(x-r\right)^{2}-4-\left(2x-1\right)=x^{2}-\left(2r+2\right)x+\left(r^{2}-3\right)=0$$

$$\Delta(r)=\left(2r+2\right)^{2}-4\left(r^{2}-3\right)=8r+16$$

The squares in $r$ cancel, so the condition is a first-degree equation with one solution.

$$8r+16=0\implies r=-2$$

At that shift the difference becomes $\left(x+1\right)^{2}$, a perfect square touching zero once.

Exactly one shift makes the line tangent, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Missing each other means a negative discriminant, and the discriminant just computed increases steadily with the shift.

$$\Delta(r)=8r+16$$

$$r<-2\implies \Delta(r)<0$$

Taking $r=-3$, for instance, leaves no real solution.

$$\Delta(-3)=-24+16=-8<0$$

Pushed far enough to the left, the parabola has slid out from under the rising line and the two curves share nothing.

Sufficiently negative shifts separate the graphs, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The formula is already in vertex form, so the turning point can be read straight off it.

$$g_r(x)=\left(x-r\right)^{2}-4\implies\text{vertex}=\left(r,-4\right)$$

The shift appears in the bracket only, which moves the vertex sideways; the constant $-4$ outside the square is the height, and $r$ never enters it.

$$r=0\implies\text{vertex}\left(0,-4\right)\qquad r=5\implies\text{vertex}\left(5,-4\right)$$

The vertex height stays $-4$ for every shift, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The axis of symmetry is the vertical line through the vertex, and vertex form puts the vertex at abscissa $r$.

$$g_r(x)=\left(x-r\right)^{2}-4\implies\ell:\;x=r$$

The mirrored values confirm it, since only the distance from $r$ enters the square.

$$g_r\left(r+t\right)=t^{2}-4=g_r\left(r-t\right)$$

Changing $r$ therefore drags the axis along with the whole graph.

The axis moves exactly as much as the shift, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The crossing with the vertical coordinate axis is the value at $x=0$, so substitute and see whether the shift survives.

$$g_r(0)=\left(0-r\right)^{2}-4=r^{2}-4$$

The result depends on $r$, and two members already disagree.

$$r=0\implies g_{0}(0)=-4\qquad r=3\implies g_{3}(0)=5$$

Sliding a parabola sideways changes the height at which it passes the $y$-axis.

The family crosses the $y$-axis at different points, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: $g_r-f=x^{2}-(2r+2)x+(r^{2}-3)$ with discriminant $8r+16$: tangency at $r=-2$.

tasks.title: Rebuild from a Vertex and a Point
tasks.context: The line $f$ has slope $-3$ and passes through the point $(1,2)$. The quadratic $g$ has leading coefficient $2$ and its vertex at $(2,-8)$. Recover both formulas, then judge the statements. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The roots of $g$ are $0$ and $4$.
The graphs of $f$ and $g$ meet at a point of the $y$-axis.
Matching $g=Af^{2}+Bf+C$ forces $A=\frac{2}{9}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A slope and one point determine a line, and the point-slope shape is the quickest route to its formula.

$$f(x)=-3\left(x-1\right)+2$$

$$f(x)=-3x+3+2=-3x+5$$

The check is immediate: the slope is $-3$ and the value at $x=1$ is $2$, as required.

$$f(1)=-3+5=2$$

The recovered formula is exactly the one claimed, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A leading coefficient together with a vertex determines a parabola, and vertex form assembles it directly.

$$g(x)=2\left(x-2\right)^{2}-8$$

$$g(x)=2x^{2}-8x+8-8=2x^{2}-8x$$

The constant terms cancel, which is worth checking against the vertex: the axis is at $x=-\left(-8\right)/\left(2\cdot 2\right)=2$ and the value there is $8-16=-8$.

The expanded formula matches the claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

With no constant term the recovered formula factors at sight, so the roots need no quadratic formula.

$$g(x)=2x^{2}-8x=2x\left(x-4\right)$$

A product vanishes exactly when one of its factors does, and the factor $2$ never does.

$$2x\left(x-4\right)=0\iff x=0\text{ or }x=4$$

The midpoint of the two roots is $2$, which is the axis of symmetry found from the vertex, so the two computations agree.

The roots are $0$ and $4$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A common point on the vertical coordinate axis would mean the two functions agree at $x=0$, so evaluate both there.

$$f(0)=5\qquad g(0)=0$$

The heights differ, so $x=0$ is not a meeting abscissa; solving the meeting equation confirms where the graphs actually cross.

$$2x^{2}-8x=-3x+5\implies 2x^{2}-5x-5=0$$

$$\Delta=25+40=65\implies x=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{65}}{4}$$

Neither of these abscissas is $0$, since the constant term $-5$ of that equation is non-zero.

The graphs do meet twice, but never on the $y$-axis, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Only the term $Af(x)^{2}$ can supply an $x^{2}$, so square the recovered line and compare that coefficient with the one in $g$.

$$f(x)^{2}=\left(-3x+5\right)^{2}=9x^{2}-30x+25$$

$$9A=2\implies A=\frac{2}{9}$$

The division is legitimate because the slope $-3$ is non-zero, and no other value of $A$ can reproduce the coefficient $2$; matching the $x$ term and the constant term afterwards gives $B=\frac{4}{9}$ and $C=-\frac{70}{9}$.

The leading coefficient of the rewriting is forced to be $\frac{2}{9}$, so the statement is True.

tasks.title: Axis Gap, Vieta, and Nested Order
tasks.context: Let $f(x)=3x-7$ and $g(x)=x^{2}-5x+2$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Completing the square gives $g(x)=\left(x-\frac{5}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{17}{4}$.
At the axis of $g$ the gap $f-g$ equals $\frac{19}{4}$.
By Vieta the sum of the roots of $g$ is $-5$.
The graphs of $f$ and $g$ meet at two distinct points.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Completing the square rewrites a parabola as $a(x-h)^{2}+k$, where $h$ is the abscissa of the axis of symmetry and $k$ is the height of the vertex, so both numbers have to be produced first.

$$g(x)=x^{2} - 5 x + 2$$

The axis comes from the first two coefficients.

$$x=-\frac{-5}{2\cdot 1}=\frac{5}{2}$$

The vertex height is the value of $g$ on that axis.

$$g\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)=\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)^{2}-5\cdot \left(\frac{5}{2}\right)+2=-\frac{17}{4}$$

Putting the leading coefficient, the shift and the height together gives

$$g(x)=\left(x-\frac{5}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{17}{4}$$

This is the very expression the claim displays, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The vertical gap between the two graphs at a given abscissa is the difference of the two heights there, so locate the axis of the parabola first and then evaluate both models on it.

$$x=-\frac{-5}{2\cdot 1}=\frac{5}{2}$$

Both functions are evaluated at that abscissa.

$$f\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)=3\cdot \left(\frac{5}{2}\right)-7=\frac{1}{2}$$

$$g\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)=\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)^{2}-5\cdot \left(\frac{5}{2}\right)+2=-\frac{17}{4}$$

Subtracting the parabola height from the line height gives the gap.

$$f\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)-g\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-\left(-\frac{17}{4}\right)=\frac{19}{4}$$

The gap is $\frac{19}{4}$, exactly the value claimed, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Vieta's relations connect the coefficients of a parabola with its roots directly, without solving anything: the sum of the two roots is minus the middle coefficient divided by the leading one.

$$S=-\frac{b}{a}$$

$$g(x)=x^{2} - 5 x + 2$$

$$S=-\frac{-5}{1}=5$$

The sum of the roots is $5$ while the claim reports $-5$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Nesting is not symmetric: feeding the line into the parabola need not agree with feeding the parabola into the line, so each order has to be computed on its own, working from the inside outwards.

$$f(0)=-7\qquad g\left(-7\right)=86$$

$$g(0)=2\qquad f\left(2\right)=-1$$

The two orders give $86$ and $-1$, which are different numbers, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The abscissas where the graphs meet solve $g(x)=f(x)$, so bring the line over and read the discriminant.

$$x^{2}-5x+2-\left(3x-7\right)=x^{2}-8x+9=0$$

$$\Delta=\left(-8\right)^{2}-4\left(1\right)\left(9\right)=64-36=28$$

A strictly positive discriminant makes the square root a genuine positive number, so the quadratic formula returns two different real abscissas.

$$x=\frac{8\pm\sqrt{28}}{2}=4\pm\sqrt{7}$$

Both values are real and they differ by $2\sqrt{7}$, so the line cuts the parabola in two separate points.

The graphs meet at exactly two distinct points, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The stem names a line and a parabola,

$$f(x)=3 x - 7\qquad g(x)=x^{2} - 5 x + 2$$

The turning point is worth having in hand: the axis of symmetry is read off the first two coefficients, and evaluating $g$ there supplies the height.

$$g(x)=\left(x-\frac{5}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{17}{4}\qquad \text{vertex}=\left(\frac{5}{2},-\frac{17}{4}\right)$$

Coefficients alone settle the sum $S$ and the product $P$ of the roots of $g$, and the sign of its discriminant tells how many of those roots are real.

$$S=5\qquad P=2\qquad \Delta_{g}=17$$

Wherever the two graphs touch, the difference $f-g$ is zero; that difference is quadratic and its discriminant leaves two crossings.

$$f(x)-g(x)=- x^{2} + 8 x - 9\qquad \Delta=28$$
